entries.title: OpenAI Codex on Amazon Bedrock
entries.summary: A practical guide for enterprises rolling out OpenAI Codex to developers on AWS, with Amazon Bedrock as the model backend, covering the access, governance, and cost decisions that platform, security, and finance teams need to align on.
entries.content:
Artificial Intelligence

OpenAI Codex on Amazon Bedrock

Developers increasingly use Codex with Amazon Bedrock to explore unfamiliar code, make changes, and handle repetitive engineering work. For platform teams, the challenge is to make those tools available without creating a second model-access, identity, and operations stack.

Codex can use Amazon Bedrock for inference with supported OpenAI models. In this post, we show how to fit that path into the AWS identity, AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM), Regional, and observability practices your organization already uses. Codex still runs on the developer workstation. The main design choice is how its model requests reach Amazon Bedrock and where your organization applies policy and operational controls.

We begin with a small, least-privilege pilot and work through the checks that matter before access expands. The examples use GPT-5.6 Sol. Before starting the pilot, review Supported models by AWS Region in Amazon Bedrock to confirm that Sol, Terra, or Luna is available in the AWS Region and inference path you plan to use.

Recommended default: Start with Native AWS Access for a small, least-privilege pilot. Choose AgentCore Gateway, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, when you want AWS managed gateway infrastructure for routing or Amazon Bedrock Guardrails. Choose an LLM Gateway when a platform team wants to enforce controls in the request path. A custom integration is the advanced version of the LLM Gateway pattern, not a quick start.

The examples come from the open source Guidance for Codex on AWS repository. It includes quick starts for Native AWS Access, AgentCore Gateway, LiteLLM on ECS, Portkey, the AWS Distro for OpenTelemetry (ADOT), and the Amazon CloudWatch setup used later in the post. Choose the quick start that matches your architecture, use it for the pilot, and adapt it to your environment.

Choose your rollout path

Authentication is only one part of an enterprise rollout. Decide who can use the service and which models and Regions are approved. Also define where configuration lives, what telemetry to collect, how usage is allocated, and which skills or Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers are allowed. The following table maps those needs to an access path and an owning team.

Choose the access path that provides the controls you need now. The most straightforward path that meets the requirement usually has the lowest operational overhead.

Decision rules

  • Native AWS Access is the usual starting point when AWS identity and IAM controls are enough for the pilot.
  • Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale, with any framework or model. Within the platform, AgentCore Gateway fits teams that want AWS managed gateway infrastructure for routing, Amazon Bedrock Guardrails, or related controls.
  • A large language model (LLM) Gateway fits organizations that already operate a gateway or want to enforce controls in the request path. Building a custom gateway is the advanced version of this option.

The following diagram compares where identity, routing, policy, telemetry, and operational ownership sit across the three rollout paths.

Native AWS Access

If Native AWS Access fits the pilot, the repository’s Native AWS Access quick start provides the complete procedure and supporting files. The following abbreviated walkthrough focuses on the sequence and the checks that matter most.

Use your workforce identity provider for sign-in

Employees continue to sign in through the identity provider they already use. In this example, Okta handles authentication through Security Assertion Markup Language (SAML) and provisions users and groups into IAM Identity Center through System for Cross-domain Identity Management (SCIM). IAM Identity Center then issues the temporary AWS credentials used by Codex. The identity provider is not configured in Codex.

Prerequisites

  • Add each pilot user to a dedicated group in the workforce identity system and provision that group to IAM Identity Center. Keep the assignment limited to the pilot.
  • Choose an Amazon Bedrock Region and an OpenAI model available to the pilot identity, plus an inference profile if the selected API requires one. Check Sol, Terra, and Luna separately for the chosen account, Region, and inference path.
  • Grant only the Amazon Bedrock model inference permissions used by Codex, any direct validation commands, and the selected observability destination.
  • Prepare a non-production repository and name a rollback owner.

Configure

The pilot has three checks. First, sign in using the IAM Identity Center profile configured for the AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) and call Amazon Bedrock Runtime directly. Next, point Codex to the approved model. Finally, run a safe Codex task. The direct call isolates AWS access problems. The final step confirms the Codex configuration.

Step 1: Sign in and validate Amazon Bedrock Runtime access.

This command creates a short-lived AWS session and checks whether the profile can invoke the chosen model in the chosen Region. If it fails, resolve the profile, Region, model or inference-profile access, or IAM permissions before configuring Codex.

Step 2: Configure the Codex provider.

The model value is the Codex model ID. The profile selects the AWS IAM Identity Center session, and region tells Codex which AWS Region to use. Keep these settings in user-level or managed configuration so a repository cannot change the provider.

Verify the pilot and confirm rollback

Before adding users, make sure the pilot reaches the approved model, produces the expected records, and can be disabled cleanly.

  • Identity: 
    aws sts get-caller-identity
    returns the expected IAM Identity Center assumed-role session.
  • Model access: The pilot profile invokes the approved model through the API and Region selected for the test.
  • Codex access: The user completes a safe, read-only task in a non-production repository, and the expected request-path evidence is available.
  • Evidence and rollback: The identity, invocation, audit, and optional telemetry records are present. Remove the configuration or IAM Identity Center assignment, handle any active session according to your procedure or wait for it to expire, and verify that a new invocation is denied.

Watch the Native AWS Access walkthrough

The walkthrough shows the complete pilot sequence: workforce sign-in, direct Amazon Bedrock Runtime validation, Codex provider configuration, and a safe test task.

Figure 2: Native AWS Access walkthrough covering workforce sign-in, Amazon Bedrock Runtime validation, Codex provider configuration, and a safe pilot task

Use the video to verify the order of the checks and the evidence to collect before adding more pilot users.

Run a two-user identity-isolation check

Two users are required to test identity isolation. A single user shows that sign-in works. A second user tests whether attribution remains distinct. Have two pilot users sign in separately and run the same harmless task. Their assumed-role sessions and audit records, and telemetry records if configured, should remain distinct.

The following diagram shows how separate pilot identities should produce separate AWS sessions, request evidence, and optional telemetry while using the same approved Codex and Amazon Bedrock path.

Gateway paths for request-path controls

AgentCore Gateway is an option when you want AWS managed gateway infrastructure for centralized routing or Amazon Bedrock Guardrails. If your organization already runs an LLM Gateway or wants to enforce controls in the request path, use that gateway instead. Validate the selected gateway before exposing it to pilot users.

LLM Gateway: Validate before a pilot

  • Check that the gateway accepts the Codex request format.
  • Use the sign-in or token flow defined by the gateway team.
  • Before inviting pilot users, test model routing, monitoring, failure handling, and rollback.

Custom enterprise integration

A custom enterprise integration is the most involved form of the LLM Gateway pattern. Consider it only when Native AWS Access, AgentCore Gateway, and an existing gateway cannot meet a specific requirement. The result is another service to design, secure, test, support, and operate, so platform engineering and security need to own it from the start.

Observe, govern, and allocate cost

Codex OpenTelemetry, Amazon Bedrock service records, AWS identity records, and billing data answer different questions. Codex OpenTelemetry describes client activity. Amazon Bedrock service metrics and model invocation logs show service-side activity when enabled. AWS identity records and the AWS Cost and Usage Report (CUR) provide identity and billed-usage evidence. Correlate them for the path you deploy, and do not present token volume as a cost report.

Define what code, prompts, files, and tool output Codex might send through the selected model path. Exclude secrets and restricted data unless the organization has approved that data flow. Require developers to review and test generated changes before merge. Telemetry does not establish correctness or safety.

OpenTelemetry metrics from Codex

For observability, this post uses the ADOT collector configuration and CloudWatch dashboard from the repository’s monitoring and operations guidance. Deploy that configuration to each managed pilot device, then run a safe Codex task.

The repository provides the configuration files. Follow its deployment instructions to install the approved ADOT collector and configure its AWS authentication.

Validate the repository path: run a safe Codex task and confirm that the expected operational metrics appear on the managed CloudWatch dashboard.

Telemetry planeExamplesAttribution boundary
Codex OpenTelemetry metricsToken usage, turns, API requests, request duration, tool calls, session source.Per-user and team dashboard grouping only after the local collector adds validated identity attributes.
Amazon Bedrock service metricsInvocations, latency, input tokens, output tokens, client errors, server errors.Use the documented namespace, metric names, and dimensions for the selected Runtime, Mantle, or AgentCore path.
AWS identity evidence, model invocation logs, and CURAssumed-role single sign-on (SSO) principal plus billed Bedrock line items.For Native IAM Identity Center access, CUR 2.0 with caller-identity allocation can expose the SSO principal. Gateway paths require gateway telemetry and spend records for end-user allocation.

Amazon CloudWatch dashboard and evidence

The Amazon CloudWatch Coding Agent Insights managed dashboard in the Guidance for Codex on AWS repository shows Codex operational metrics collected through ADOT. Use it to understand client activity, and use AWS identity, audit, and billing records separately when you need attribution or cost evidence.

QuestionDecisionEvidence to keep
Who invoked the model?Use the AWS identity/audit source for the path you selected.Pilot identity record and request correlation, where available.
What did it cost?Use billing data for actual charge and label any inferred allocation clearly.CUR source, allocation method, and known uncertainty.
Can we stop unsafe or expensive behavior?Use alarms for detection. Use IAM and managed client controls for their respective access and action boundaries. Use gateway policy when request-path enforcement, such as hard budgets or rate limits, is required.Control test results and rollback procedure.

Watch the Codex OTel and CloudWatch walkthrough

The walkthrough shows how to query Codex OpenTelemetry metrics and confirm that the expected token and request data appears in Amazon CloudWatch.

Figure 4: Codex OpenTelemetry metrics shown in an Amazon CloudWatch dashboard

The example validates the aliased metric result in Amazon CloudWatch Query Studio and shows how the dashboard represents Codex client activity.

Standardize team behavior

After the infrastructure path is working, turn to the developer experience. Repository guidance, managed plugins, hooks, and approved MCP servers can make the rollout consistent without asking each team to assemble its own setup.

Plugins

Organization-owned plugins are a practical way to distribute shared skills, hooks, and approved MCP integrations. Give each plugin an owner and version, review changes before release, and publish it only through approved sources. Test updates with a pilot group and keep a documented removal path.

A plugin might include an MCP server configuration, but that does not make every bundled tool approved. Allow only the servers and tools the organization has reviewed, with user confirmation where it is needed.

Hooks

Hooks can be declared in 

hooks.json
or directly in configuration. Keep the documented event casing, and deploy organization-owned policy commands through approved endpoint tooling.

Use PreToolUse, PostToolUse, or SessionStart where they solve a specific need. Before wider deployment, test allow, deny, timeout, and disconnected-endpoint behavior.

MCP

An MCP server connects Codex to another system, so each server creates a separate trust boundary. Limit access to the users and tools that need it, manage credentials through an approved OAuth or secrets process, and require confirmation for tools that change external systems. Keep MCP credentials out of the model-provider configuration.

Roll out in phases

The following diagram defines the scope and evidence required to advance from preparation through pilot, expansion, and organization-wide standardization.

Administrator launch checklist

  • Record the selected path, owning team, Region, and model in the change record.
  • Limit the pilot identity to the required permissions, and document how issued credentials or tokens are handled.
  • Run a non-production test that covers sign-in, model availability, and one safe Codex task.
  • Check telemetry and audit output from the deployed version rather than assuming the example applies unchanged.
  • Separate billed amounts from estimates in cost reporting.
  • Exercise recovery: remove the configuration or assignment, handle any active session through the approved procedure or wait for it to expire, and verify that a new invocation is denied.

Clean up

When the pilot ends or access must be disabled, remove the rollout resources that are no longer required.

Remove the Codex model-provider and telemetry configuration from managed devices. Remove the IAM Identity Center pilot assignment or gateway access, revoke pilot tokens and secrets, and handle active sessions according to the approved procedure. Uninstall or disable the ADOT collector, and delete the pilot CloudWatch dashboard and alarms if they are not shared with another workload. Verify cleanup by confirming that a new model invocation is denied and that retired telemetry resources receive no new data.

Configuration boundaries

Keep model-provider, credential, and organization telemetry settings in user-level or managed configuration. Project-local 

.codex/config.toml
is repository-scoped configuration: Review it as code, but do not treat it as an enterprise enforcement boundary. AGENTS.md is useful for durable repository guidance, such as test commands and coding conventions, but it is not an enforcement boundary either.
Setting typeRecommended locationReason
Model provider, credentials, RegionUser-level or managed configurationThese are endpoint and enterprise choices, not repository defaults.
OpenTelemetry exporterUser-level or managed configurationTelemetry destination and data handling are organization controls.
Repository instructionsAGENTS.mdCarries durable guidance but is not an enforcement boundary.
Permission requirementsOrganization-managed 
requirements.toml
 Constrains supported security-sensitive client choices.

Conclusions and next steps

Codex can use Amazon Bedrock for inference with supported OpenAI models. Start with the least-complex access path that meets the requirement, prove the identity and model path with a small pilot, and add gateway or client controls only when they solve a specific need.

AgentCore Gateway provides an AWS managed gateway option for routing or Amazon Bedrock Guardrails. Choose an LLM Gateway when a platform team wants to enforce controls in the request path. Build a custom integration only when the available paths cannot meet a documented requirement.

Expand in stages and use evidence from each stage to decide what comes next. The Guidance for Codex on AWS repository contains the maintained configurations and validation procedures used in this post.

entries.title: Semantic diffing of formal policies with anti-unification
entries.summary: A textual diff of two formal policies flags every cosmetic change and hides the one that alters behavior. This post shows how to compute a symbolic, deterministic semantic diff with an open-source anti-unification engine, so reviewers see only the genuine disagreements between two candidate authorization policies.
entries.content:
Artificial Intelligence

Semantic diffing of formal policies with anti-unification

When reviewing code, you start with a diff. You wouldn’t compare two 3,000-line files by eye and hope to spot every change. Formal policies can be even harder to compare because a textual diff often highlights syntactic changes that don’t affect meaning. Reorder two conjuncts, swap the arguments of an equality, or use an equivalent predicate, and much of the file might appear changed. A real change in behavior, such as an 

Or
where the requirement says and, can get lost in that noise.

A semantic diff shows what two policies have in common and where they disagree. The open source engine used in this post computes this diff using anti-unification, which finds a most specific common pattern for two expressions. Plotkin’s 1970 paper gives the classical formulation. The engine works over an e-graph, which keeps track of expressions known to be equal. We supply the algebraic laws and domain rules that justify those equalities, such as equating an external destination with one that isn’t internal. The result shows the shared parts once and keeps both versions of each differing part for review. If no differences remain, the policies are equivalent under those laws and rules. When the rules or the search are incomplete, a remaining difference might reflect an equivalence the engine has not found.

One use case is autoformalization. Autoformalization translates natural language into a formal language. Suppose you want to turn requirements into SMT-LIB, the standard input language for satisfiability modulo theories (SMT) solvers such as Z3 and cvc5, or into Cedar or Dogwood to control authorization in your software system. A large language model (LLM) generates the formal artifact from the prose. The model writes the artifact. It plays no part in computing the diff. Run the model twice, and it might produce two different formalizations, with no ground truth to identify the correct one. A semantic diff shows where they agree and where they differ. Generate more candidates by varying the model, prompt, or sampling temperature. Comparing them shows which parts stay the same and which vary. Review the varying parts first.

Requirements can also become OpenShell sandbox policies or Common Expression Language (CEL) expressions. OpenShell uses YAML to describe an agent’s filesystem and network access. CEL is embedded in applications to evaluate expressions, including policy conditions. These languages and formats differ in what they express, but translations into any of them can disagree about a condition, a scope, or an event. The following table gives illustrative disagreements:

Language or formatPolicy focusExample disagreement
Cedar Who can perform an action on a resource, under which conditions.One translation requires ownership and approval. Another accepts either.
Dogwood Authorization involving the current request and recent event history.One translation checks a successful prior response. Another checks a request event.
OpenShell policies An agent’s filesystem and network access, including rules for particular binaries.One translation permits repository-scoped 
GET
. Another permits organization-scoped 
POST
.
CEL Conditions evaluated over inputs supplied by a host application.One translation requires production for both allowed ports. Another requires it for only one.

In each worked example, we compare translations of the same requirement within one policy context. We encode the relevant syntax as terms and declare the equalities used in the comparison. The engine reads these encodings. It doesn’t import native policies from the four formats.

The idea is a formal-methods analogue of semantic entropy, described by Farquhar et al. in Nature (2024). That approach samples several natural-language answers, clusters those that entail one another, and reports a single number. For formal outputs, anti-unification preserves more information. It identifies the shared structure and each divergence instead of returning only a score.

Counterexamples help explain the consequences of a disagreement. An SMT solver can find a concrete assignment that satisfies one formula and violates the other. A reviewer can then trace that assignment through the formulas to understand the conflicting decisions. The anti-unifier gives a different view: it organizes the shared structure and the fragments that differ, without issuing an SMT query. A solver or policy validator can help resolve those fragments. We assume you can read S-expression syntax, as in SMT-LIB, and know what an authorization policy is. E-graphs and anti-unification are explained as they come up.

When several translations agree on part of a requirement, the diff shows that part once. Where they disagree, it keeps the alternatives visible for review.

How semantic diffing represents disagreement

Say a policy-generation pipeline hands you two candidate rules for this requirement: sensitive data sent to an external destination must be encrypted.

Rule ARule B

sensitive(data) ∧ external(dst) → encrypted

¬internal(dst) ∧ sensitive(data) → audited

Whether these are the same rule isn’t obvious. The conditions are reordered, external is expressed indirectly as not internal, and the conclusions do not match. The engine computes a most specific anti-unifier for these terms. In its input language, the two rules are S-expressions.

The complete program first declares the vocabulary:

It then adds one 

function
line for each predicate (
sensitive
, 
external
, 
internal
) and constant (
data
, 
dst
, 
encrypted
, 
audited
). Here, 
And
is declared associative, commutative, and idempotent, as the next section explains:

The engine answers with a single term:

The reordering doesn’t appear in the result because 

And
is declared associative, commutative, and idempotent. Two 
Variants
nodes remain, each marking a place where the inputs disagree, and only one of them is a difference in meaning. The difference between 
(external dst)
and 
(Not (internal dst))
is a difference in vocabulary. Both express the same domain fact. The engine can’t infer that from syntax alone. State the domain fact as a 
rewrite
, run it to saturation (until no rule adds a new equality), and diff again:

After saturation, the engine answers:

One 

Variants
node remains: Rule B audits where the requirement demands encryption. A textbook presentation would put a fresh variable at that spot. The engine instead writes 
(Variants encrypted audited)
: a node that holds both readings. Select the first child of every 
Variants
node and you reconstruct rule A, up to the declared algebra and rewrites. Select the second child and you get rule B. The anti-unifier is a lossless merge of both terms: Shared structure appears once, and every genuine disagreement is a localized, reviewable node.

Three fields describe the result: 

:size
, 
:cr
, and 
:completion
. The 
:size
field counts the concrete nodes (a 
Variants
marker itself isn’t counted, but both of its children are, so structure can’t hide inside one).

The 

:cr
field reports the compression ratio 
(s - a) / b
, where 
s
is the result size and 
a
and 
b
are the smaller and larger input sizes. For each input, we use its smallest known equivalent form in the current e-graph. A score of 0 means full agreement under the declared equalities.

After the preceding rewrite, both inputs have seven nodes and the result has eight, giving 

(8 - 7) / 7
, or approximately 0.1429. Keeping both complete policies in a single 
Variants
node would use fourteen nodes, giving 
(14 - 7) / 7 = 1
. This is the reference value for no sharing.

A score of 1 is a reference value, not an upper bound. The search might use larger equivalent forms than the smallest known inputs. A result larger than their combined sizes therefore scores above 1. For example, if both smallest input forms have ten nodes and a result has twenty-three, the ratio is 

(23 - 10) / 10 = 1.3
.

The 

:completion
field reports 
exact
when the search space was exhausted and 
budget
when the default anytime search (a Monte Carlo search, described in the implementation section) reached its playout limit before exhausting the search space.

A low 

:cr
means the inputs share more structure under the declared equalities. It doesn’t establish correctness: two candidates can share the same mistake. An entropy score summarizes variation in one number. The full semantic diff also identifies where the candidates disagree and retains both alternatives in 
Variants
nodes.

A semantic diff ignores only the differences covered by the declared equalities. A plain syntactic anti-unifier would also have reported the reordering in this example. The next three sections show how to declare the algebra and add domain identities.

The anti-unifier stores shared structure once and marks each disagreement with a Variants node. Selecting one side of every node reconstructs the corresponding input, modulo the declared equalities.

Run a semantic diff in 5 minutes

The engine requires only a pinned Rust toolchain to build from source. Its formal-verification annotations, covered in the implementation section, compile away under plain 

rustc
. These commands pin the revision used for the worked examples:

It prints a single 

(anti-unify ...)
term.

The command-line interpreter reads one S-expression file (

.egg
by convention). You declare sorts and operators, define two terms with 
let
, optionally add rewrite rules and run them to saturation, and issue 
antiunify
. Two mechanisms tell the engine which syntactic changes do not affect meaning: annotations that assign algebraic properties such as associativity, commutativity, and idempotence to operators, and explicit rewrite rules for everything else. Here is the algebraic part of the signature used in the worked example:

And
and 
Or
are variadic, associative, commutative, and idempotent, and each has a Boolean neutral element. 
Eq
is commutative. Every reordering, regrouping, and duplication of conjuncts therefore counts as the same term. Nothing else is assumed: Only the stated laws hold, and any further identities must be written as explicit rewrites. The 
:identity
element is what lets the diff align a conjunct that one input has and the other lacks: The missing conjunct is paired with 
(Lit true)
rather than causing the entire 
And
expression to fail to align. Both case studies rely on this identity alignment.

:assoc-comm-idem makes reordered, regrouped, and duplicate operands equivalent. :identity lets the diff align a missing operand with the operator’s neutral element.

Worked example with two policy bugs

The running example ships with the repository as egraph/examples/au_policy_divergence.egg. Consider one policy sentence:

A cross-Region replication request is permitted only if the source bucket has versioning enabled and the destination bucket lies in an approved Region. If the object is tagged confidential, the destination and source accounts must be the same and server-side encryption with a customer managed key must be in effect. Objects up to the multipart threshold are copied directly. Larger objects require a multipart copy.

Two people, or two independent runs of the same model, produced formalizations of it (

formulaA
and 
formulaB
in the file):
Encoding AEncoding B

Five things differ textually. Three are presentational: The conjuncts are reordered, the 

Eq
arguments are swapped, and 
approvedRegion
is explicitly expanded into two AWS Regions (
us-east-1
and 
eu-west-1
). Two involve different operators: An 
And
became an 
Or
in the confidential clause, and 
Lte
became 
Lt
at the size threshold. A unified diff of the two encodings marks 18 of their 28 lines as changed (Figure 1, textual-diff pane) and gives no indication of which of the five differences change meaning. The exact anti-unifier of the two encodings follows:

Two of the five differences disappear. The conjunct reordering is absorbed because 

And
is declared associative, commutative, and idempotent (ACI). The swapped 
Eq
arguments have the same printed order in both readings because 
:comm
canonized them. Neither changes meaning, so neither is reported.

The confidential clause uses 

Or
where the requirement says and. Encoding A requires both the same-account check and server-side encryption with a customer managed key. Encoding B accepts either. The engine aligns A’s conjunction with B’s disjunction through their neutral elements, so the disagreement surfaces as two adjacent 
Variants
nodes. Choose the first child at each node to reconstruct A: The 
Or
collapses onto the plain equality, and 
sseCmk
remains a mandatory conjunct. Choose the second child at each node to reconstruct B: The mandatory 
sseCmk
weakens to 
(Lit true)
and survives only as an alternative inside the 
Or
. Together, the two 
Variants
nodes show that encoding B accepts server-side encryption alone and therefore admits cross-account replication of confidential objects.

You might have expected 

sseCmk
to be shared rather than repeated. However, a first-order anti-unifier can’t generalize the connective itself, so 
And
versus 
Or
forces the split into two alignments. Identity alignment still shares the five-node equality once. The exact solver’s exhaustive search finds no smaller form, and the printed result is one node smaller than holding both clauses whole in a single 
Variants
.

Add the domain 

rewrite
and run the diff again. The 
Variants
node for the Region is not a bug. It reflects missing domain knowledge: In this deployment, the approved Regions are exactly those two. State that as a 
rewrite
, saturate, and diff again:

The Region difference moves into the shared backbone, and 

:cr
drops from 0.5862 to 0.4000. The full result is the semantic-diff pane of Figure 1. Exactly two disagreements remain: the weakened confidential clause and the threshold. B’s 
Lt
is strict, so an object exactly at 
multipartThreshold
is copied directly under A and takes the multipart path under B. The divergence is confined to the 
Ite
condition. Both branches sit in the shared backbone. Both surviving differences are genuine bugs that an authorization reviewer must resolve. The algebra and one domain rewrite account for the other differences. The same file also runs the anytime search, 
(antiunify formulaA formulaB :algorithm uct :playouts 3000)
, which returns the identical size-35 term. The whole program completes in well under 100 ms on an Apple M3 Pro laptop (50–60 ms after the binary is warm). That covers parsing, declarations, saturation, five anti-unification queries with their regression checks, and process startup. We measured the wall-clock time of 
./target/release/semi-persistent egraph/examples/au_policy_divergence.egg
using a release build at Rust 1.97.1 and the shell’s 
time
command over five warm runs. The Get started section shows the same command.
textual diff: 18 of 28 lines flaggedsemantic diff: two disagreements, localized

Figure 1: The same pair of encodings under diff and anti-unification. On the left, the textual diff flags 18 of 28 lines (removed, added). On the right, one domain rewrite moves the shared structure into the gray backbone, and the highlighted Variants confine the remaining differences to the weakened confidential clause and the strict threshold. The semantic-diff pane wraps one long line to fit

After applying the declared algebra and one domain rewrite, the five textual differences reduce to two semantic disagreements: the weakened confidential clause and the strict size threshold.

Semantic diffing for Cedar and Dogwood policies

In an authorization policy, a dropped guard widens what is permitted and can cause the policy to fail open. Cedar is the open source authorization policy language behind Amazon Verified Permissions. Dogwood extends Cedar authorization policies with temporal conditions for runtime verification of AI agents. Its temporal sublanguage uses recorded event history to guard an action. The engine doesn’t evaluate Dogwood policies. It diffs their abstract syntax modulo a declared algebra. Validation (schema checking) and replay (evaluating a policy against a recorded event history) remain Dogwood’s job. The engine’s user guide has a worked chapter that diffs two independently produced Dogwood candidates for one requirement:

The agent may POST to /deploy, but only if a health check has already come back 200 in the last 15 minutes.

Candidate A keeps both request guards (method and path) but reads the status code from a request event, an event kind that carries no such field. Candidate B uses the correct response event but drops the 

/deploy
path guard. After any matching health check, B also permits a 
POST
to 
/admin/purge-all
. The candidates differ in six additional presentational ways, all of which the declared algebra or a three-rule comparison theory absorbs:
Presentational differenceAbsorbed by
Cedar condition order

versus

The comparison theory consists of three visible rewrites, not a hidden normalization pass:

The anti-unifier of the two candidates (doc/book/examples/20-dogwood-simple.egg in the repository) has size 61, 

:cr
0.1864, and exactly two disagreements in an otherwise shared policy backbone:

Use the simplest available check for each disagreement. Two binary disagreements give four candidate completions. Dogwood validation resolves the first without human review by rejecting both request completions (“predicate … mentions field 

output.status_code
, which is not declared on that event”). The second disagreement is an identity alignment: Candidate A’s path guard pairs against 
eTrue
, showing that candidate B omitted the guard. The requirement resolves it (keep the guard), and a replay covering two decision points shows the consequence: After a health check, candidate B allows the off-target 
POST
, whereas the repaired policy denies it. Combining B’s event kind with A’s guard produces a policy that neither candidate wrote. Choosing between the candidates would have kept one of the two bugs.

Commutativity has a side condition, and the engine doesn’t check it. Cedar’s 

&&
short-circuits, so commuting it is sound only when neither operand can raise an error. The comparison therefore relies on validation to rule out order-dependent errors, such as an attribute access that is safe only behind a 
has
guard. The engine doesn’t re-check that condition.

A canonical printer can remove the presentational differences, but it can’t recover a dropped guard. A canonizing printer plus textual diff can absorb most, arguably all, of the six differences in the table more cheaply. No normalizer can align a two-conjunct condition against a three-conjunct one inside an otherwise matched term. Matching modulo the identity element aligns them by pairing the dropped conjunct with 

eTrue
. In a 
permit
condition, that dropped conjunct exposes the widening that makes the policy fail open.

For the Dogwood candidates, the algebra and three rewrites remove six presentational differences. The remaining disagreements expose a schema error and a dropped guard. Combining the correct choices produces a policy that neither candidate supplied.

Comparing policy translations: OpenShell and CEL

The next two examples adapt predicates from the OpenShell and CEL articles. For each, we construct candidate translations of the same requirement. These are illustrative encodings, not recorded LLM samples.

OpenShell: Method and path scope. The OpenShell example models network permissions as predicates over a binary, host, port, layer, method, and path. We adapt the article’s reduced SMT-LIB model, whose path condition is a prefix test. We use that vocabulary for this requirement:

Allow inspected REST requests made by /usr/bin/gh to api.github.com on port 443 when the method is GET and the path begins with /repos/NVIDIA/OpenShell/issues/. Deny all other requests.

Candidate A requires 

GET
and the repository’s issues prefix. Candidate B uses 
POST
and the broader 
/repos/NVIDIA/
prefix. The other checks appear in a different order. In the encoding, 
gh
, 
github
, and 
https
name the binary, host, and port shown earlier. The names 
issuePrefix
and 
orgPrefix
identify the two prefixes. The exact solver returns:

The binary, host, port, and layer checks are shared. Their ordering disappears because 

And
is declared associative, commutative, and idempotent. Two 
Variants
nodes identify the conflicting readings: the permitted operation and the path scope. The requirement settles both choices here. For an ambiguous requirement, the same nodes would give its owner two specific alternatives to resolve.

CEL: The scope of a shared condition. The CEL example exposes a production check lost during refactoring. We reuse the expressions as candidate translations of this requirement:

Allow a request exactly when it is in production and its port is either 80 or 443.

CEL’s 

&&
binds more tightly than 
||
, so candidate B applies the production check only to port 80. We encode the expressions with supplied Boolean and integer inputs, using 
isProd
, 
port80
, and 
port443
for the corresponding input and literals:

The port-80 branch is shared. In the port-443 branch, 

(Variants isProd (Lit true))
shows the missing production condition. At 
is_prod = false
and 
port = 443
, A denies the request and B allows it. The diff directs the review to one part of the sentence: whether “in production” applies to both alternatives.

This example assumes that 

is_prod
is supplied as a Boolean and 
port
as an integer. Under these assumptions, neither expression raises an error. The encoding doesn’t model CEL errors or unknown values, and the engine doesn’t check these input assumptions.

CEL-Java’s verification framework can check equivalence and policy invariants with Z3. Such checks can provide evidence when resolving a disagreement. The anti-unifier itself doesn’t decide which translation matches the requirement, and a mistake shared by both candidates would remain shared.

Implementation and performance

The algorithm runs over an e-graph, a data structure that stores a term together with everything it is known to equal. E-graphs (equivalence graphs) come from congruence-closure procedures in theorem provers and were popularized for compiler optimization by equality saturation, as described by Willsey et al. in “egg: Fast and Extensible Equality Saturation” (POPL 2021). This engine’s e-graph adds native canonization for associative and commutative operators.

Anti-unification over e-graphs is also used for abstraction learning and program compression in babble (Cao et al., POPL 2023). Earlier implementations didn’t scale beyond small examples. Our saturation-based prototype also stalled there. Native AC canonization, AC-aware matching over distinct children, and direct search made subsecond queries practical. Semi-persistence reduced the cost of repeated queries.

Native AC canonization. Associativity, commutativity, and idempotence are not rewrite rules in this engine. They are properties of the data structure. Associative-commutative (AC) operators store their children as canonical sorted multisets (ACI operators as canonical sorted sets) at insertion time. One e-node therefore represents all reassociations and permutations of a term and, for idempotent operators, treats duplicate children as one. Equality modulo the declared laws is structural equality. The rewrite-based alternative floods the e-graph with an exponential family of equivalent copies before real work starts.

AC-aware matching over distinct children. Pattern matching against multiset nodes uses maximum-partition semantics: It branches over the distinct children of a node rather than enumerating multiplicity splits, so heavily repeated arguments do not cause a combinatorial blowup.

Direct search instead of rewriting. Anti-unification itself isn’t encoded as rewrite rules either. An exact dynamic programming solver (

:algorithm exact
) solves the joint-decomposition problem optimally. Optimal here is relative to its size-first objective, the current e-graph, and the configured cycle policy. An anytime Monte Carlo graph search (
:algorithm uct
, the default) returns its best answer for any playout budget. On the worked example’s pair, 3,000 playouts reproduce the exact optimum. Both optimize first for result size and then, among equal-size answers, prefer those that retain more structure in the shared backbone.

Semi-persistence. The e-graph supports 

(push)
and 
(pop)
snapshots recorded as sparse diffs rather than deep copies. Restoring a state therefore costs work proportional to what changed because the snapshot, plus the cost of repairing derived indexes. Proportional-cost restore lets the engine compare many candidates over one shared graph. A backtracking search can restore an earlier state without copying the full graph.

A verified core and its scope. The e-graph’s underlying container layer is verified in Verus, a verifier for Rust. The verified property is that restore reproduces the state at the matching 

(push)
(1,703 verified conditions, 0 errors). The anti-unification crate proves its objective-order and lower-bound lemmas, but the full solver doesn’t yet have an end-to-end refinement proof. The engine can log a justification for every equivalence it derives (
--proofs
). As the repository notes, these records aren’t yet independently replay-checked certificates. All of these claims, with evidence tiers and retractions, are in the repository’s claims inventory (doc/claims.md).

Native canonization avoids materializing equivalent AC terms. Distinct-child matching controls multiplicity, direct solvers avoid encoding anti-unification as rewrites, and semi-persistence reduces the cost of repeated queries.

Using semantic diffing in a pipeline

The same method extends from two candidates to a larger sample. Generate N candidate formalizations of the requirement. Load them into one shared e-graph, saturate under your domain rules, and cluster them using pairwise equality checks. In the user guide’s larger Dogwood study, five samples collapse into three clusters. Candidates that differ only in presentation join the same equivalence classes during construction. Anti-unify the cluster representatives pairwise. Then, in a layer built on top of the engine’s output, group recurring 

Variants
nodes by their position in the shared backbone. In the study, three pairwise diffs reduce to exactly two review items. Use the simplest available check for each item: schema validation, replay, example I/O pairs, or human review.

With 

(push)
and 
(pop)
snapshots, you can test a proposed resolution without rebuilding the graph. Temporarily assert one branch of a 
Variants
node as a domain fact, run the diff again, and roll back. A tool built on top of the engine could select and repair a full candidate against hard and soft constraints, for example with a MaxSMT solver over the variant space. MaxSMT (maximum satisfiability modulo theories) seeks a solution that satisfies all hard constraints while satisfying as many soft constraints as possible, or maximizing their total weight. Section 8 of Programming Z3 describes this form of optimization. That capability is not part of the current engine. Figure 2 summarizes the pipeline.

Use a semantic-diff budget in continuous integration (CI). The command 

(checkau A B :max_size N :algorithm exact)
prints nothing on success and causes the program to fail when the anti-unifier exceeds the budget. Every printed result in the user guide is pinned this way, so the guide and the engine can’t drift apart. The same command can serve as a regression gate. Set a maximum result size for a reference formalization and a regenerated one, and fail the pipeline when the anti-unifier exceeds it. The binary follows standard shell conventions: Results go to 
stdout
, diagnostics (
ok --- N nodes
) go to 
stderr
, and the process exits non-zero if any check fails.

The diff can also guide a follow-up prompt or a question to the requirement owner. Mean pairwise 

:cr
across samples gives a disagreement score for each requirement. A 
Variants
node already contains the alternatives needed for a specific clarification, such as “did you mean strictly less than the threshold, or at most?”

With several candidates, cluster equivalent outputs, compare the cluster representatives, and resolve recurring disagreements with validation, replay, examples, or human review.

Get started

Build the engine at the revision used for this post, then run the policy examples. These commands select the revision containing the OpenShell and CEL examples from pull request 103:

The engine is Apache-2.0 on GitHub. The user guide progresses from basic terms to the policy case studies, and the test suite runs every program in it directly from the repository. Annex B documents the 

antiunify
and 
checkau
commands. If your artifact language has an abstract syntax tree (AST) and an equational theory, you can diff it: Declare the algebra, state the domain identities as rewrites, and ask for the most specific anti-unifier. If your policies are Cedar, whether handwritten or generated for Amazon Verified Permissions, the same recipe applies to them. The OpenShell and CEL examples show how to encode other policy constructs and compare candidate readings of a requirement.

entries.title: Detecting and recovering from silent data corruption on Amazon SageMaker HyperPod
entries.summary: Silent data corruption is a GPU fault that returns wrong but plausible numbers with no error, quietly poisoning distributed training. This post adds three checks to a PyTorch DDP loop to detect it, localize the faulty node on Amazon SageMaker HyperPod, and hand the node to automatic recovery for replacement.
entries.content:
Artificial Intelligence

Detecting and recovering from silent data corruption on Amazon SageMaker HyperPod

Silent data corruption (SDC) happens when hardware, such as a GPU, returns a wrong but plausible number and raises no error. In distributed training, the wrong number can flow into the gradients and weights of every replica. Loss can still look normal for hours, and by the time a team notices an unexplained divergence or a weaker model, the compute is spent. It happens at scale: during a 54-day period of Llama 3 405B pre-training on up to 16K H100 GPUs, Meta attributed 6 of 419 unexpected job interruptions to silent data corruption, and those were only the cases that interrupted the job and were traced to SDC.

Amazon SageMaker HyperPod already replaces nodes that report a fault: the health-monitoring agent watches for GPU errors, deep health checks stress-test nodes, and automatic node recovery swaps out bad hardware. SDC slips past all of these features, because the hardware never reports anything. Detection has to come from the training job itself.

In this post, we add three checks to a PyTorch DistributedDataParallel (DDP) training loop to detect SDC. When a check fires, we map the suspect rank to its node, contain the corruption, and have SageMaker HyperPod replace the node. Each check covers a different place where a fault can land:

  • A non-finite gradient check catches NaN, Inf, and overflow in a GPU’s forward or backward pass, on the step it happens, and NaN or Inf that the gradient all-reduce introduces.
  • A ring replay audit catches finite wrong values. On audit steps, every GPU recomputes a micro-batch from another node and compares the loss bit for bit and the gradients by fingerprint.
  • A weight fingerprint comparison catches corruption in the optimizer step and in stored weights, by comparing every replica’s weights after the update.

We tested the checks with software-injected faults on a SageMaker HyperPod cluster with 4 ml.p5.48xlarge instances (32 NVIDIA H100 GPUs), and repeated every test on three instances, the minimum the checks need. The full code of this solution is available in the accompanying GitHub repository.

How silent data corruption happens and why the usual checks miss it

SDC comes from manufacturing defects (marginal transistors that slip past vendor screening) and silicon aging in a specific compute unit, most often a multiply-accumulate lane in a tensor core, which is exactly the hardware model training hammers. That marginal circuit computes correctly most of the time and wrong only under stress: high temperature, voltage droop, or specific operand patterns. Because the arithmetic logic path has no ECC or parity (unlike memory), the wrong result, say 4.0001 instead of 4.0000, is never flagged, and it flows through activations and gradients into every replica’s weights.

The reason it is so hard to catch is that SDC is in the compute path, and every integrity check you already have guards a different boundary:

CheckWhat it guardsWhy it misses SDC
ECCmemoryCatches bit flips in memory, not wrong math. There is no ECC on a tensor-core result.
Xid errors (NVRM)GPU driver/hardware faultsThe GPU raises an Xid when it detects a fault. SDC by definition raises none, so nothing lands in 
/aws/sagemaker/Clusters/
HMA logs.
DCGM deep health checkhardware faultsMisses defects that need your workload’s operands, thermal state, or timing. Runs on an idle node, outside your job.
NVLink / PCIe / EFA checksumstransportVerify bytes arrived as sent, not that they were computed correctly.
Checkpoint checksumsstorage round-tripA poisoned-but-consistent checkpoint checksums fine.

The way to catch SDC is to check the result of the computation itself.

Solution overview

The loop has four steps. Your training job does the first two, and the last two use Kubernetes and SageMaker HyperPod features:

Step 1. Detect: Three checks in your training loop name a suspect GPU by comparing data-parallel replicas.

Step 2. Localize: On SageMaker HyperPod clusters orchestrated by Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS), the Kubernetes node name contains the instance ID, so mapping a suspect rank to a node is a lookup.

Step 3. Contain and correlate: Stop the job, cordon the node, and look at its GPU metrics in the SageMaker HyperPod observability dashboards.

Step 4. Confirm and recover: Confirm when the alarm is ambiguous, replace the node after review, and resume from a checkpoint saved before the suspect window.

It helps to see the loop as layers, each adding something different:

LayerSourceWhat it addsCatches truly silent SDC?
1. Non-finite gradient checkYour training scriptNames a GPU whose local gradient is NaN or Inf, before the all-reduce, and stops the step if the reduced gradient is NaN or InfOnly faults that become NaN, Inf, or overflow
2. Ring replay auditYour training scriptEvery GPU recomputes another node’s micro-batch and compares the loss bits and gradient fingerprintsYes, for finite compute-path faults that change the loss or a gradient, on audit steps
3. Weight fingerprint comparisonYour training scriptNames a replica whose weights differ from a strict majority after the updateYes, for optimizer-step and stored-weight faults on one copy. Blind to compute-path faults and to sharded weights
4. LocalizationYour training script, using SageMaker HyperPod node namesMaps a suspect rank to an instance ID from the Kubernetes node namen/a: it localizes
5. DCGM correlationHyperPod observability add-onThe suspect GPU’s DCGM metrics around the alarmIt confirms faults only where they also appear in hardware counters. Clean telemetry doesn’t clear a node.
6. Deep health check
StartClusterHealthCheck
(DCGM L4)		 An on-demand hardware diagnostic on the suspect nodeIt catches hardware defects its own test patterns trigger. Triage, not proof
7. Repeat-offender historyA query you build over retained alarms and telemetryNodes that alarm repeatedlyPartly: it surfaces nodes worth checking early

Layers 1–3 are the only layers that detect silent SDC, and they live in your training code. Layer 4 turns their alarm into an instance ID, and the HyperPod layers corroborate the alarm and close the loop.

Prerequisites

To follow along, you need:

  • A SageMaker HyperPod cluster orchestrated by Amazon EKS, with at least three GPU nodes. The ring audit needs three different nodes for every comparison it settles, and the weight comparison needs three copies of each weight to name the odd one out. See Orchestrating SageMaker HyperPod clusters with Amazon EKS.
  • A PyTorch DDP training job in which every replica runs its own optimizer step, with a data pipeline that can rebuild any rank’s micro-batch for a given step, such as a seeded sampler.
  • Checkpoints on shared storage, Amazon FSx for Lustre or Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3). Replacing a node destroys its root and secondary volumes, including anything on local NVMe.
  • The SageMaker HyperPod observability add-on for the correlation step. Turn on advanced DCGM metrics if you want ECC, NVLink, and throttling counters.
  • Access to the cluster through 
    kubectl
    , and AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) permissions for 
    sagemaker:StartClusterHealthCheck
    and 
    sagemaker:BatchReplaceClusterNodes
    . See Manually quarantine, replace, or reboot a node.

Step 1: Detect with three checks in your training loop

Data parallelism trains several copies of the model, called replicas, at the same time. Each replica trains on a different slice of the batch. After each backward pass, an all-reduce averages the replicas’ gradients, and every replica applies that same average in 

optimizer.step()
. Here’s one weight across three replicas, with a learning rate of 0.1:
replica 0replica 1replica 2
weight at start0.5000.5000.500same
local gradient0.200.400.30different (different data)
averaged gradient0.300.300.30same, after the all-reduce
weight after step0.4700.4700.470same

Local gradients differ, because each replica sees different data. And after the optimizer step, the weights must be identical, bit for bit.

Where a fault lands decides which check can see it. If replica 1 computes a local gradient of 4.00 instead of 0.40, the all-reduce spreads that error to every replica: all three apply the same wrong update, and their weights still match. Only replica 1’s local gradient looked different, and only before the all-reduce. If instead replica 1 corrupts a weight during or after the optimizer step, its weights no longer match the others. There’s one exception: a NaN or Inf in one replica’s weights reaches every replica through the next all-reduce, and after that the replicas agree again. A fault inside the all-reduce itself, such as a GPU that adds a partial sum wrong, also reaches every replica identically.

So compute-path faults must be caught before the optimizer step, while the bad gradient can still be discarded, and faults in the update or in stored weights after it. Finite wrong values need recompute: comparing gradient norms across replicas catches only NaN and Inf (see Why not compare local gradient norms?). That gives three checks on every DP rank, in a fixed order within each training step:

  • Non-finite gradient check – Before the all-reduce, flag any rank whose local gradient is NaN or Inf. This catches values that blow up in a GPU’s forward or backward pass, on the step they happen, and names the GPU. After the all-reduce, check the reduced gradient for NaN or Inf too, before the update.
  • Ring replay audit – On audit steps, before the optimizer step, every rank recomputes the micro-batch of a rank on another node. It compares the loss bit for bit and, with deterministic kernels, every parameter’s gradient fingerprint. This catches finite wrong values in the compute path.
  • Weight fingerprint comparison – After the optimizer step, every N steps and before every checkpoint, compare every replica’s weight fingerprints. This catches faults in the optimizer step and in stored weights.

The code in this step is for PyTorch DDP. For tensor, pipeline, or context parallelism, see Beyond DDP.

Order of execution

Why not compare local gradient norms?

A natural first design, and the one we started with, flags a rank whose local gradient norm is more than k median absolute deviations (MADs) from the median of that step. We recorded every rank’s local gradient norm on every step of the three fault-free runs on 4 instances (22,800 steps, see Fault-free runs) on 32 H100s training a 953-million-parameter model, and the test doesn’t work:

  • The healthy spread is too wide – Each rank sees different data, so healthy local norms already reached 224 MADs in the first 800 steps, and 1,240 MADs over all healthy steps.
  • A quiet threshold sees nothing finite – At k = 336, 1.5 times the highest score in the first 800 healthy steps, it raised 11 false alarms in the remaining 22,000 healthy steps. And no finite fault came close: the faulty rank’s score never exceeded 6.9, even with one activation multiplied by 10,000.

Compare by fingerprint

Checks 2 and 3 compare tensors across GPUs. Sending whole tensors would cost too much, so each tensor is reduced to a fingerprint: two 64-bit sums of its raw bit patterns, one plain and one weighted by position. Any change to one or two elements of a tensor changes the fingerprint, for tensors with fewer than 2³² elements of up to 4 bytes each. That covers every weight fault we injected. Larger changes could, in principle, cancel out, so equal fingerprints are strong evidence of equal tensors, not proof. The position-weighted sum matters: in our tests, a swap of two weight values and a compensating change to two values left the plain sum unchanged, and only the weighted sum caught them.

Check 1: NaN/Inf gradients, before and after the all-reduce

A DDP communication hook records each rank’s local gradient before it’s averaged. It stores the squared norm of every gradient bucket and, on deterministic audit steps, the fingerprints of every parameter’s gradient (used by check 2). Then it passes the bucket to PyTorch’s standard all-reduce.

After backward, 

nonfinite_ranks
gathers one scalar from every rank and returns the ranks whose local gradient norm is NaN or Inf. The first rank flagged is the faulty one. If the step were applied, the NaN would reach every rank on the next step.

train()
also checks the gradient after the all-reduce. A NaN or Inf produced inside the reduction reaches every replica the same way, so the copies still match and check 3 passes them. Without this check, the NaN becomes NaN weights on every replica, and a checkpoint due on that step is saved with them and tagged as passing. 
clip_grad_norm_
already computes the norm of the reduced gradient, so the check adds only one one-element all-reduce per step. A finite error in the reduction still passes every check.

If you train with fp16 and a gradient scaler, exclude the overflow steps the scaler already skips. bf16 doesn’t have them.

Check 2: Ring replay, before the optimizer step

Every replica holds the same weights until 

optimizer.step()
. So, between the backward pass and the optimizer step, any rank can recompute any other rank’s micro-batch, and with deterministic kernels it must get the same bits.

On an audit step, every rank r recomputes the micro-batch of rank r + 8: 8 positions ahead, which is one node away on p5 instances. It uses the unwrapped module, so nothing is all-reduced, and it restores the gradients, the module’s buffers, and the random-number state afterwards. A replay blocks the job no matter how many ranks do one, so auditing every rank costs the same wall-clock time as auditing one.

Each rank then appears in two comparisons: its own micro-batch, replayed by a peer, and the micro-batch it replayed for someone else.

  • Both comparisons mismatch: That rank computed wrong in both, so it’s the culprit.
  • Only one mismatches: Either side could be wrong. 
    confirm
    settles it in place: the GPU eight positions after the target, on a third node, and the target itself replay the target’s micro-batch again. That also tells a persistent fault, which the target reproduces, from a transient one, which it doesn’t.

The confirmation is only independent if the three GPUs are on three different nodes. 

check_topology
verifies that for every pair before training starts, from each pod’s 
NODE_NAME
, and raises an error otherwise.

Choose the audit mode:

  • Default kernels: Compare the loss only. This needs a forward pass whose loss is bitwise reproducible, which held in our tests: healthy replays matched the original loss bit for bit. Gradients can’t be compared this way, because attention’s default backward pass isn’t deterministic. This mode catches forward-pass faults that change the loss.
  • Deterministic kernels (
    deterministic_audits=True
    ): The whole audit step runs with deterministic algorithms and the math attention kernel. Gradient fingerprints then match too, so the audit also catches backward-only faults. An op with no deterministic implementation raises an error instead of producing a false alarm. On our model, a deterministic audit step cost 2.4 times a default one.

Never replay a suspect’s work on the suspect alone. A GPU with a persistent defect can reproduce its own wrong answer.

Check 3: Weight fingerprints, after the optimizer step

After 

optimizer.step()
, every replica’s weights must be identical, so there’s no tolerance to tune. Each rank fingerprints every weight tensor and gathers everyone’s fingerprints.

A rank is named only when its copy of a tensor differs from a strict majority, more than half of the copies. With two copies, or a split with no strict majority, the comparison reports a disagreement without naming any rank.

Run it every N steps and on every checkpoint step. It’s the only check that runs after the update, so it’s the only one that can stop a checkpoint from being written out of a corrupted copy. In our tests, a weight corrupted right after one update was caught at the next checkpoint step, and the save didn’t happen. Without the forced check, the save went ahead from the corrupted copy, and the ring audit noticed only at the next audit, five steps later.

It costs 31.1 ms per check on a 953-million-parameter model: 2 percent of a step when it runs every 10 steps.

Put the checks in the training loop

train
runs each step in the order of Figure 2 and stops at the first alarm. It decides whether a step is an audit step before the forward pass, because a deterministic comparison needs the original computation to be deterministic too. When check 1 or 2 fires, it zeros the gradients and returns without clipping or applying the update, so the bad gradient never reaches the weights or the optimizer state, and the exact state is still there for confirmation. After clipping, it checks whether the reduced gradient is NaN or Inf, and if it is, returns before the update. It saves a checkpoint only if nothing fired.

The alarm’s 

suspect_window
is the range of steps since the last pass of the check that fired. A fault that was active on every step since it started began inside it. An intermittent fault can be older, and a fault that no check sees can be in any checkpoint, so treat the tags as a record that the checks passed at that step, not as proof that the saved state is clean.

A training script calls it like this:

The replay depends on these:

  • Exact micro-batches: 
    rebuild_batch(step, rank)
    must return exactly the micro-batch that rank trained on, for example from a seeded sampler.
  • Same loss function: 
    compute_loss
    must be the same function in training and in replay, including autocast, and any randomness inside it, such as dropout, must be seeded per step and rank.
  • No collectives or output-affecting state in the model: The confirmation replay runs on only two ranks, the target and the third GPU, so a model that calls a collective inside its forward or backward pass (SyncBatchNorm, for example) hangs on an ambiguous alarm. A buffer that the forward pass both reads and updates makes a healthy replay differ.
  • Deterministic setup: Set 
    CUBLAS_WORKSPACE_CONFIG=:4096:8
    before the training process starts, and make sure every op in the model has a deterministic implementation.
  • Peer offset: Number DP ranks node by node, so that 
    peer_offset
    equal to the GPUs per node puts every replayer on another node. 
    check_topology
    refuses a layout where it doesn’t.
  • Untested here: Unused parameters, gradient accumulation, BatchNorm, and forward hooks with side effects. With unused parameters, set 
    deterministic_audits=False
    , which compares the loss only.

audit_every
is the main cost-versus-robustness setting:
  • Detection delay: A persistent finite fault is caught within 
    audit_every
    steps if it also occurs in the kernels the audit runs. Deterministic audits run deterministic kernels and the math attention kernel, so a fault confined to the default kernels used on the other steps is never audited.
  • Corrupted updates: Up to 
    audit_every
    − 1 corrupted updates can be applied before the audit catches it. They’re inside the alarm’s 
    suspect_window
    .
  • One-time faults: A finite fault on a single non-audit step that doesn’t recur isn’t caught at all.

Make 

ckpt_every
a multiple of both 
audit_every
and 
check_every
, so every checkpoint step is audited before its update and fingerprinted after it.

We measured the average step time end to end, over 1,000 consecutive steps per schedule, on the 953M model and 32 H100s. Every schedule with the checks also runs the weight check every 10 steps:

ScheduleAverage step timeOver plain DDP
Plain DDP, no checks157.4 ms—
Checks, no audits169.0 ms+7.4%
Deterministic audits every 10 steps211.9 ms+34.7%
Default-kernel audits every 10 steps177.0 ms+12.5%
Deterministic audits every 100 steps173.3 ms+10.1%
Default-kernel audits every 100 steps169.3 ms+7.6%

About 7 percentage points of each schedule’s cost don’t depend on audits: the gradient hook and the two NaN/Inf checks on every step, and the weight check every 10 steps. A reasonable starting point for production is deterministic audits every 100 steps, which cost 10 percent here. They still catch a persistent fault within 100 steps, including a backward-only one, at the price of up to 99 corrupted updates to roll back. Audit every 10 steps when you need faster detection, for example during a burn-in on new capacity or while you watch a suspect node. Measure the cost on your own model: deterministic attention uses the math kernel, whose cost grows with the square of the sequence length.

In the fault-free runs, 15,320 audit steps and 3,080 weight checks raised no alarm, which bounds the false-alarm rate at about 1 in 5,100 audit steps (95 percent confidence).

Step 2: Localize the suspect rank to a node

A rank is a logical ID. To act on it, you need the instance and the physical GPU. On HyperPod EKS, the Kubernetes node name is the instance ID with a 

hyperpod-
prefix. Pass it to your pod with the Kubernetes downward API:

At job start, log a table that maps every rank to its node, instance, and GPU UUID:

If a job is already running without the downward API, you can map a pod to its node from outside with 

kubectl get pod  -o jsonpath='{.spec.nodeName}'
.

Step 3: Contain the damage and check the GPU metrics

When an alarm fires, stop the job first. Then stop new work from landing on the suspect node by cordoning the node while you investigate:

Then open the GPU health dashboard in the SageMaker HyperPod observability add-on, filter to the suspect node and GPU, and look at the time the alarm fired. A rise in correctable ECC errors, PCIe replays, throttling, or temperature on that GPU raises confidence that the hardware is at fault. A clean panel doesn’t clear the node: pure SDC often leaves no trace in hardware telemetry.

Step 4: Confirm, then replace the node

With the Step 1 checks running, an alarm already names a suspect GPU. When you see a symptom without an alarm, such as a loss spike, or want to rule out software before you replace anything, start with the cheap explanations. Most loss spikes aren’t SDC, and chasing SDC on a data bug wastes days:

The test that separates SDC from software is whether the problem follows the hardware:

  • A reproducible failure doesn’t rule out SDC – Meta pinned a failing workload to one core and got the same wrong answer every time for specific inputs.
  • Neither does a failure that starts at a software change – Google traced one incident to a correct library update that began using rarely used instructions on defective cores.
  • Don’t expect the global loss to point anywhere – A forward fault first changes the faulty rank’s own loss, and the all-reduce then spreads its gradient to every replica. Per-rank checks and replays give you the locality.

Decide what the alarm means

AlarmMeaningSuggested action

suspects is None

culprits == [r]

Verdict persistentThe target reproduced its own wrong answer, and a third GPU agreed with the replayerKeep cordoned. Replace after review
Verdict transientThe target’s retry came out right and agreed with the third GPU. An intermittent fault can look the sameKeep cordoned until an audit with the node as the target, or a deep health check, passes. Replace it if it happens again
Verdict replayer computed wrongThe replaying GPU, not the target, was wrongTreat the replayer as the suspect, and confirm again

check == "reduced gradient"

Verdict unattributable or unclearThe three GPUs don’t line upAmbiguous: check DCGM and run deep health checks on the nodes involved

In production, keep a human approval on every replacement until you have evidence of the checks’ precision on your own workload. Synthetic tests like ours don’t establish it.

Confirm an ambiguous alarm

A deep health check is the main tool for ambiguous alarms. Its stress tests catch faults that the hardware reports, and subtle data-dependent faults often pass. To run one on the suspect instance group:

Replace the node

When you’re ready to replace the node, you have two options. Both trigger the same SageMaker HyperPod recovery process, described in Manually quarantine, replace, or reboot a node.

If automatic node recovery is turned on, you can label the node and let SageMaker HyperPod replace it, which is convenient for automation:

To use the API instead, run:

On clusters that use Karpenter for autoscaling, 

BatchReplaceClusterNodes
terminates the node but creates a replacement only if pending pods need one. After the replacement joins, the training job restarts through the SageMaker HyperPod training operator or the job’s restart policy, and your training script resumes from the newest checkpoint saved before the alarm’s 
suspect_window
starts. Call 
find_divergent_ranks
right after loading it, before the first step. Replacement destroys the node’s root and secondary volumes, so keep checkpoints on shared storage.

Automating the workflow

The manual steps are for understanding. In production, wrap them in a small controller that runs in your own cluster and account:

  • Trigger: The training job reports the alarm as a Kubernetes event, a small custom resource (for example SDCReport{rank, job, step, check}), or an Amazon CloudWatch alarm on metrics such as 
    sdc_nonfinite_grad
    , 
    sdc_replay_mismatch
    , and 
    sdc_divergent_tensors
    .
  • Resolve: The controller maps rank → pod → node through the Kubernetes API, then node → instance ID by stripping the 
    hyperpod-
    prefix.
  • Contain: It cordons the node.
  • Decide: It applies the table in Step 4. The ring audit has already confirmed ambiguous pairs in place, so the alarm carries the verdicts. For an ambiguous result, it runs one node-scoped deep health check.
  • Recover: For a replacement, it asks a human to approve, then calls 
    BatchReplaceClusterNodes
    , or sets the node-health label if automatic node recovery is turned on. Then it relies on the training operator and your checkpoint reload, and records every step in CloudWatch.

Build it as a lightweight Kubernetes operator, or as an Amazon EventBridge rule on the CloudWatch alarm that invokes an AWS Lambda function.

Use case: Testing the checks on SageMaker HyperPod

We ran the tests twice on one SageMaker HyperPod cluster orchestrated by Amazon EKS, using 4 and then 3 ml.p5.48xlarge instances with 8 NVIDIA H100 80GB HBM3 GPUs each, and PyTorch 2.9.0 (CUDA 13.0) from the AWS Deep Learning Containers training image. The model was a 953-million-parameter Llama-style decoder with 16 layers, a hidden size of 2,048, 16 attention heads, a 32,000-token vocabulary, and 2,048-token sequences. Each GPU processed 2 sequences per step (131,072 tokens per step on 32 GPUs), with fp32 weights, gradients, and optimizer state, and bf16 autocast for compute. We trained with AdamW at a learning rate of 3 × 10⁻⁴ after a 100-step linear warm-up, with betas of (0.9, 0.95), weight decay of 0.1, and gradient clipping at 1.0. The data was synthetic: a copy task with Zipf-distributed tokens whose first half repeats, seeded per rank and step so that any micro-batch can be rebuilt.

Fault scenarios

Faults were injected in one layer, the MLP down-projection of the eighth of 16 decoder blocks, on a chosen rank and step:

  • Forward faults change the layer’s output but keep its gradient path, like a wrong multiply in the forward pass.
  • Backward-only faults change the gradient of the layer’s input or weight.
  • Weight faults change one GPU’s copy of the stored weight right after the optimizer step: a bit flip, a swap of two values, or a compensating change to two values.
  • A persistent fault recurs in everything the faulty GPU computes, including the replays it runs for other ranks. A transient fault fires once.

Every scenario restarts from a snapshot taken after 400 warm-up steps, and step numbers count from it. Unless noted, audits ran every 10 steps with deterministic kernels, weight checks every 10 steps, and a checkpoint every 20. The table shows the 4-instance results. On 3 instances, every scenario raised the same alarm, at the same step, from the same check, naming the same ranks. Only the peer ranks changed.

Fault-free runs

To measure false alarms, we trained without faults on both cluster sizes, with three schedules each. Every schedule ran the weight check every 10 steps and saved no checkpoints, and each run’s length was fixed in minutes, so the two schedules that audit every step contribute most of the audit steps:

4Default kernels, every step22.55,4005,4005400

With 0 alarms in 15,320 audit steps, the rule of three puts a 95 percent upper bound of 3 / 15,320, about 1 in 5,100, on the false-alarm rate per audit step. The NaN/Inf checks didn’t fire on any fault-free step either. The gradient-norm analysis in Why not compare local gradient norms? uses the 4-instance runs only.

Beyond DDP

The weight comparison isn’t limited to DDP. 

find_divergent_ranks
takes any data-parallel group, so it also applies to tensor, pipeline, and context parallelism, HSDP, and mixture of experts, which are all layouts that keep independent copies of each weight. It can’t help under ZeRO-1 or full FSDP sharding, where each shard’s update is computed on only one rank. We tested the checks and the training loop in this post only with DDP.

To use it in another layout, call 

find_divergent_ranks
with the group that holds copies of the same shard. With only two copies, it can detect a disagreement but can’t name the faulty copy.

If you’d rather have the service check your nodes for you, SageMaker HyperPod also offers the MultiNodeTraining deep health check. It runs a short, fixed distributed training job across a batch of GPU nodes, with no code changes, and replaces nodes whose training loss turns NaN or Inf, diverges, or doesn’t finish in time. Select it alongside InstanceStress and InstanceConnectivity when you create an instance group, or run it on demand with 

StartClusterHealthCheck
. It complements the checks in this post: use it to screen new and replacement nodes before your job lands on them, and the in-job checks to catch wrong values in your own training that never become NaN or Inf. For details, visit SageMaker HyperPod Deep Health Checks.

Clean up

To avoid ongoing charges, delete what you created for testing. If you created a HyperPod cluster, delete it with 

aws sagemaker delete-cluster --cluster-name
. That removes only the HyperPod resources. Delete the EKS cluster, its add-ons, and any Amazon FSx volumes separately, after the HyperPod cluster. See Deleting a SageMaker HyperPod cluster.

Conclusion

In this post, we showed how to detect silent data corruption in data-parallel training and how to hand a suspect node to SageMaker HyperPod for replacement. Three checks cover the three places a fault can land: a NaN/Inf check on each rank’s gradient and on the reduced gradient, a ring replay that compares every GPU’s work with a GPU on another node, and a weight fingerprint comparison after the update. Run the first two before the optimizer step, don’t apply a step that failed a check, and compare weights before every checkpoint. Node names on SageMaker HyperPod EKS clusters turn the suspect rank into an instance ID. Then quarantine the node, roll back to a checkpoint from before the suspect window, and let the node-health label or the Replace API complete the recovery.

To get started, review the SageMaker HyperPod resiliency features for Amazon EKS, and try the companion repository. To go deeper, see deep health checks and the observability add-on.

entries.title: Introducing the Web Search API on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
entries.summary: Today we're announcing the Web Search API on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore: your own code can search the web with a single signed API call, with no gateway and no resources to create. Call it from the AWS SDKs or the AWS CLI and use it in applications, agent loops, and data pipelines.
entries.content:
Artificial Intelligence

Introducing the Web Search API on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore

AI agents and applications that answer questions about recent events, product releases, prices, or regulations need information newer than their model’s training data.
