Until now, Web Search on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore delivered that information to agents through AgentCore Gateway, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. That means creating a gateway and a web search target and calling the tool from an MCP client. The setup fits platform teams that share one search policy across many agents, but it’s more than you need when your own code only requires search results.

Today, we’re announcing the Web Search API on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. With it, your own code can search the web with a single API call. It returns ranked results from a web index that Amazon operates, each with a text extract and, when available, the page title, URL, and publication time. You call it from the AWS SDKs or the AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI), signed with the same AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) credentials you use for your other AWS services. There are no resources to create first. Authenticate, call, and get results. Use it in an application, an agent loop you write yourself, or a data pipeline.

Why a standalone API?

The AgentCore Gateway is the recommended path for most agentic workloads. It gives agents one secure Model Context Protocol (MCP) endpoint that combines web search with your other tools. It also handles inbound and outbound authentication, semantic tool selection, and optional MCP sessions. But developers told us they also need a lower-level integration point for scenarios where the gateway is not the right fit:

  • Custom orchestration frameworks – Developers building their own agent loops, or using frameworks like LangChain or LlamaIndex, want to call web search directly as a tool within their orchestration logic rather than routing through a gateway.
  • Non-agent use cases – Not every application that needs web grounding is an agent. Search-powered dashboards, fact-checking pipelines, content enrichment workflows, and monitoring systems all benefit from real-time web results without requiring agent infrastructure.
  • Tighter control over the request lifecycle – Some developers want to manage retries, caching, and error handling themselves rather than delegating to the gateway.
  • Simpler integration for existing applications – Applications that already have their own API layer can call the Web Search API directly, adding web grounding without adopting the full AgentCore Gateway stack.

The Web Search API complements the gateway. It runs on the same search infrastructure that powers Alexa+, Kiro, Quick, and other Amazon products, with the same quality and compliance posture, exposed as a direct API operation.

How it works

The Web Search API is the InvokeWebSearch operation on the 

bedrock-agentcore
data plane, the same endpoint that other AgentCore tools such as AgentCore Browser, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, use. Requests are signed with AWS Signature Version 4 (SigV4) from your standard AWS credentials, so there’s no API key or secret to manage.

The numbered steps are:

  • Your application calls 
    InvokeWebSearch
    with the AWS SDKs or the AWS CLI, which sign the request with SigV4 using its AWS credentials. From a virtual private cloud (VPC), the call can go through an interface VPC endpoint.
  • The API checks with AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) that the caller has 
    bedrock-agentcore:InvokeWebSearch
    on the AWS managed web search tool.
  • The API applies the filters in the request: the domains to include or exclude and the publication time range.
  • The API searches a web index that Amazon operates. Queries are served inside AWS and aren’t sent to a third-party search engine.
  • The API returns up to 
    maxResults
    ranked results, each with a text extract and, when available, the page title, URL, and publication time.

The calling identity needs one IAM permission on an AWS managed resource. It’s the same action and resource that a gateway’s service role uses for web search, so one policy covers both routes. For details, see Grant permission to call the API.

A first search request

The following example searches two trusted domains for pages published in 2026, in the US West (Oregon) Region (us-west-2), with the AWS SDK for Python (Boto3):

Every result has a text extract. The title, URL, and publication date come back when the index has them, so read them with 

get
. One result from a live call, shortened:

That’s the full integration. If your code runs on AWS Lambda, Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS), Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2), or Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS), the execution role provides credentials automatically. Add the permission to that role, and the same code runs unchanged.

Key API features

  • Domain filtering – Include or exclude specific domains to scope search results to trusted sources (for example, only aws.amazon.com and kubernetes.io for an assistant focused on AWS). Each list holds up to 100 domain names, and a root domain also matches its subdomains.
  • Date filtering – Restrict results to a publication time range with 
    publishedAfter
    and 
    publishedBefore
    , given as RFC 3339 date-times in UTC such as 2026-01-01T00:00:00Z. Both bounds are inclusive.
  • Configurable result count – Request between 1 and 25 results per query. If you don’t set 
    maxResults
    , the API returns up to 25. The search text, 
    searchQuery
    , can be up to 200 characters.
  • Results with text extracts – Each result includes a text extract and, when available, the page title, URL, and publication time, ready to feed into your model’s context window.

Getting started in under 5 minutes

Here are two ways to get a first result:

Option 1: AWS CloudShell (no local setup)

  • Open AWS CloudShell in your browser. It uses the credentials of your console session.
  • Your role will have the 
    bedrock-agentcore:InvokeWebSearch
    permission, from the preceding policy or from the broader AWS managed policy BedrockAgentCoreFullAccess.
  • Run:

Option 2: Local development

  • Install the AWS CLI, or the AWS SDK for your language. For Python, use Boto3 1.43.127 or later.
  • Create an IAM role with the preceding policy.
  • Get credentials for that role: assume it from your application or an AWS CLI profile, or sign in with it through your identity provider.
  • Run the preceding Python example, or call the API from any AWS SDK.

There’s no resource to create and no API key to manage. Authenticate, call, and get results.

Using the Web Search API with agent frameworks

The Web Search API fits naturally into popular agent frameworks. LangChain agents get it through the AgentCore web search tool in langchain-aws 1.9.3 and later:

The tool can also hold rules that the model can’t change, such as domains to exclude, a date floor, and a search budget. It returns its results as data that your code can check. For a complete example, see the daily dependency watch sample. It researches three package ecosystems in parallel with LangGraph, and checks every finding against its sources before it reports anything.

If you prefer to wrap the call yourself, a plain LangChain tool works too:

Without a framework, the WebSearchClient in the AgentCore Python SDK wraps the same call and returns results with parsed dates. langchain-aws 1.9.3 and the AgentCore Python SDK 1.26.0 add Web Search API support, so install those versions or later.

Enterprise controls, built in

Because the Web Search API uses standard IAM authentication, you get enterprise controls from the first call:

  • IAM policies. Grant or deny 
    bedrock-agentcore:InvokeWebSearch
    per user, group, or role. Use service control policies (SCPs) to enforce guardrails across accounts.
  • AWS CloudTrail logging. CloudTrail records 
    InvokeWebSearch
    requests as data events. Data events aren’t logged by default, so add an event selector for the 
    AWS::BedrockAgentCore::WebSearch
    resource type to a trail or event data store. Events record the web search tool and 
    maxResults
    , not the search text or filters. For details, see Log AgentCore Web Search API calls with AWS CloudTrail.
  • VPC support. Use AWS PrivateLink to route API calls over your private network rather than the public internet. For setup and endpoint policies, see Private connectivity with AWS PrivateLink later in this post.
  • Compliance. For a list of compliance programs that cover AgentCore, see Compliance validation for Amazon Bedrock AgentCore.
  • Searches stay in AWS. Queries are served from a web index that Amazon operates and aren’t sent to a third-party search engine.
  • Acceptable use. The Web Search Tool terms also apply to API results, including the requirement to retain and display the source citations and links that come with each result. For details, see the Web Search API Acceptable Use documentation.

Quotas apply per account. For the defaults and how to request an increase, see Quotas for Amazon Bedrock AgentCore.

By default, each account can send up to 10 requests per second in each Region, and you can request an increase. For details, see AgentCore Web Search Service Quotas.

Private connectivity with AWS PrivateLink

Agents and pipelines that handle sensitive data often run in private subnets with no route to the internet. With AWS PrivateLink, that code can call the Web Search API through an interface VPC endpoint in your VPC. Traffic between your VPC and the API stays on the AWS network, and you don’t need an internet gateway, a NAT gateway, or a proxy to reach it.

The numbered steps are:

  • Your application calls 
    InvokeWebSearch
    at the API’s standard Regional name. With private DNS, that name resolves to the interface endpoint in your subnet.
  • The endpoint policy applies, and the request reaches the API over the AWS network.
  • The API checks with IAM that the caller has 
    bedrock-agentcore:InvokeWebSearch
    , including any 
    aws:SourceVpce
    condition.
  • The API applies the request’s filters and searches the Amazon-operated web index.
  • The results return through the endpoint to your application.

To set it up, create an interface endpoint for the AgentCore data plane service, 

com.amazonaws..bedrock-agentcore
, in each VPC and Region that calls the API, and turn on private DNS:

With private DNS turned on, the API’s standard Regional name, 

bedrock-agentcore.us-west-2.amazonaws.com
, resolves to the endpoint’s private IP addresses inside your VPC. The Boto3 and AWS CLI examples in this post run unchanged, with no endpoint URL to set. The endpoint’s security group must allow inbound HTTPS (port 443) from the resources that call the API.

PrivateLink also gives you controls on top of IAM:

  • Endpoint policies – A VPC endpoint policy applies to 
    InvokeWebSearch
    requests in addition to your IAM policies, so you decide which principals can search through the endpoint. The same endpoint also carries the other AgentCore data plane APIs, such as AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, Memory, Identity, Browser, and Code Interpreter. If workloads in the VPC call them too, add statements that allow those calls. The following policy lets only one role call the API through the endpoint:
  • Require the private path – Add an 
    aws:SourceVpce
    condition to the IAM policy that grants the permission. The role can then search only through your endpoint, and the same call from outside the VPC is denied:
  • Network-level control – Security groups and subnet placement decide which instances, containers, and functions can reach the endpoint at all.

PrivateLink works the same way in every Region where the Web Search API is available. Interface endpoints are billed at standard AWS PrivateLink pricing. For details, see Call AgentCore Web Search through AWS PrivateLink.

Try it in the console

You can try the Web Search API in the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore console before you write any code. In the navigation pane, under Connections, choose Web Search.

  • Configure. In the Configure panel, set:
    • Max results: how many results each query returns, from 1–25. The console starts at 10.
    • Published date: a date range in 
      YYYY/MM/DD
      format. Only results published inside it come back. Leave it empty to include results from any date.
    • Domain filtering: up to 100 domains to include and up to 100 to exclude. Choose View and manage domains to edit the lists.
  • Test. Enter a query of up to 200 characters in the Test Web Search API panel. Each query calls the Web Search API with your settings. The panel shows how many results came back and how long the call took. For each result it shows the title, a text snippet, the publication date and the source URL. Figure 4 shows a search for “How do I set up Amazon S3 lifecycle rules?” with results limited to 
    aws.amazon.com
    and 
    docs.aws.amazon.com
    .
  • Integrate. When the results look right, you have two options:
    • Generate code snippet: get code that calls the API with the same settings, ready to paste into your agent or application.
    • Create gateway target: add Web Search as a tool on an AgentCore Gateway, so agents can call it through MCP.

The console signs each call with your own IAM identity, so your role needs the 

bedrock-agentcore:InvokeWebSearch
permission.

When to use the API compared to the gateway

ScenarioRecommended path
Building agents with MCP-compatible toolsAgentCore Gateway
Several tools behind one MCP endpoint, with optional MCP sessions AgentCore Gateway
One administrator source policy for many agents and teamsAgentCore Gateway
MCP clients that need search, such as Claude with the AWS Web Search connectorAgentCore Gateway
Custom orchestrationWeb Search API
Non-agent use cases (dashboards, pipelines)Web Search API
Want direct control over retries and cachingWeb Search API
Adding web search to an existing applicationWeb Search API

Both paths search the same index. They differ in a few ways. A gateway can also authorize callers with a JSON Web Token (JWT), while the API authorizes with IAM only. On a gateway, an administrator can set domain lists on the target that apply to every request without the calling agent seeing them. With the API, each request carries its own filters. The field names differ too: the API takes 

searchQuery
, 
publishedAfter
, and 
publishedBefore
, and the gateway’s MCP tool takes 
query
, 
from
, and 
to
. For more guidance, see Choose between the API and the Gateway connector.

Pricing

The Web Search API meters to the same usage type as the gateway connector, so it’s billed at the Web Search rate of $7 per 1,000 queries. Because no gateway is involved, there are no gateway charges. For details, see Amazon Bedrock AgentCore pricing.

Availability

The Web Search API is available in the US East (N. Virginia), US East (Ohio), US West (Oregon), Europe (Ireland), Asia Pacific (Tokyo), and Asia Pacific (Sydney) Regions. For the current list, see Supported AWS Regions.

Get started

Use the following resources to help you get started.

entries.title: ICYMI: What landed for AI builders in October 2026
entries.summary: A recap of the major Amazon Bedrock, Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, and Strands updates from October 2026: new models to match each task, updates that keep agents available and grounded, and clearer cost reporting for AI builders.
entries.content:
Artificial Intelligence

ICYMI: What landed for AI builders in October 2026

At AWS, we believe AI builders should be able to choose the right model for every task, trust their agents in production, and see clearly what their AI workloads cost. That belief guides how we invest across our portfolio. Amazon Bedrock gives you access to leading models and the tools to build and scale AI applications securely. We extend this foundation with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, which provides the platform to build, connect, and optimize agents using any model and any framework. That includes Strands, our open source agent development toolkit. Together, they take you from first prototype to production.

As agents move into core business workflows, the bar rises. You need the flexibility to use different models as tasks, budgets, and latency targets change. When a primary model is throttled or unreachable, your agents must keep working. They also must act within limits you set and return output other software can use as is. Their answers must stay grounded in sources you allow, and their cost must hold up at high volume.

What we shipped in October addresses each of these needs. New models help you match each task to the right price and speed, from high-volume subagents to real-time voice. Amazon Bedrock and AgentCore updates keep agents available, hold them to the processes you define, and help you trust what they return. New pricing and cost reporting make spend more predictable. Strands adds new ways to build, contain, and test agents.

Match the model to the task on Amazon Bedrock

Run fast, low-cost subagents. Claude Haiku 5.5 is built for subagents and high-volume, cost-sensitive work. According to Anthropic, it is the most capable Haiku yet and costs around 75 percent less than Claude Haiku 4.5 for most tasks. It is also the first Haiku with effort controls, so you can tune cost against intelligence for each task. In a multi-agent setup, a model such as Claude Opus 5.5 can plan the work and hand well-defined coding, tool use, and browser automation tasks to Haiku. This keeps running many agents in parallel affordable.

Get near-flagship results at a lower price. OpenAI GPT-6.1 Terra is now generally available on Amazon Bedrock. On OpenAI’s Agents’ Last Exam evaluation, it performed on par with GPT-6 Astra and completed tasks more than three times faster than GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol. Its input and output token prices are at least 50 percent lower than those of GPT-6.1 Sol and GPT-5.6 Terra. It accepts text and images with up to 1 million input tokens, which suits drafting proposals, interpreting technical drawings, and building agents that work across business systems. For latency-sensitive work such as real-time coding assistants, GPT-6.1 Sol now also offers Ultrafast mode.

Build voice agents that reason in real time. Amazon Nova 2.5 Sonic, our latest speech-to-speech model, improves reasoning, instruction following, and tool-calling accuracy, with lower latency at the same price as Amazon Nova 2 Sonic. A customer service agent can now look up an order, check return eligibility, and start a return in a single conversation.

Pick specialized models for coding and video. GLM 5.3 by Z.ai is an open-weight model for agentic coding and long-horizon software engineering, with a 1-million-token context window and prompt caching, available to eligible enterprise customers. TwelveLabs Pegasus 1.5 turns entire videos into structured, time-coded metadata. It reads visuals, audio, and on-screen text in a single pass, with no separate ingestion pipeline.

Use more models in AWS GovCloud (US). Claude Haiku 5.5 and OpenAI GPT-5.6 models with cross-Region inference are now available in AWS GovCloud (US). Daybreak Red from OpenAI, a model for authorized security work, is available to eligible customers in AWS GovCloud (US-East). Regulated teams get more models while maintaining US data sovereignty.

Build and run agents you can rely on

Build and operate agents from your terminal. AgentCore CLI, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, is now generally available in version 1.0. We rebuilt it with faster startup, a consistent command structure, and support for more AgentCore resources. You can work with harnesses, runtimes, memory, identity, gateways, and payments directly or through a project. Existing projects move to version 1 with one command. The result is one tool from local development to day-to-day operations.

Keep agents available when a model is throttled. AgentCore Gateway, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, now supports the Amazon Bedrock InvokeModel APIs and model fallback. Your existing Amazon Bedrock SDK code can point at the gateway without per-provider code changes. When the primary model is throttled or unreachable, the gateway routes the request to the next model or provider in a chain you define. A circuit breaker skips destinations that are failing. The gateway can also reach private targets in your virtual private cloud (VPC) using certificates from your own private certificate authority. Your agents stay available without retry logic in every client.

Turn your business workflows into agent tools. You can now use AWS Step Functions workflows, including your existing Standard and Express workflows, as tools through AgentCore Gateway. Your business logic stays in a workflow you already run and trust, so you don’t rebuild it inside the agent or rely on a prompt to follow it. The agent decides when to run a workflow, and Step Functions runs each step exactly as you defined it. For example, a support agent can start your refund workflow, and every refund still goes through the same eligibility check, approval, and credit steps.

Get JSON your systems can use as is. Structured outputs are now available for all Claude models on Amazon Bedrock. You receive schema-compliant JSON without custom parsing or retries. You can extract every required field from an earnings report, or route support tickets with entities that always match your data model.

Keep answers grounded in sources you trust. Web Search on Amazon Bedrock now supports domain filtering and user location for requests made with the OpenAI Responses API. You can allow up to 100 domains, block up to 100 domains, and return results relevant to a geography. Amazon Bedrock Guardrails then checks that answers stay true to their sources. Its new Standard tier for contextual grounding checks costs the same as the Classic tier, covers conversational and reasoning responses, and supports more languages. With both, you can control where answers come from and catch hallucinations in more of your applications.

Predict and lower the cost of running agents

Pay for agent memory based on what you use. AgentCore memory, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, now prices short-term memory by the data your agents ingest, retrieve, and store, instead of a flat rate per event. Most workloads see lower costs, and small-payload use cases see the largest reductions. You can also set a time-to-live on long-term memory records to meet retention requirements and control storage costs.

See what drives your Amazon Bedrock spend. AWS Cost Explorer, AWS Budgets, and AWS Cost Management Dashboards now break down Amazon Bedrock cost by model, model provider, inference type, and feature, at no additional charge. Finance and platform teams can find their most expensive models or set a budget alert for a single model, in the billing tools they already use. To lower input costs, Advanced Prompt Optimization can now also shorten your prompts, returning a shorter version only when it scores at least as high on your evaluation.

Build voice, local, and well-tested agents with Strands

Ship voice agents in a few lines of code. Strands Bidi Agents, for building two-way, speech-to-speech voice agents, are now generally available, with direct support for Amazon Nova Sonic, OpenAI, and Gemini models. Bidi Agents reconnect to the model in the background, so long calls keep going past a provider’s session limit. A voice agent can also hand longer work, such as research, to another agent and explain the results aloud.

Let local agents work within your limits. Strands Box, now in developer preview, is an open source local sandbox for AI agents. It combines operating-system isolation with semantic policy. You set policy for each tool, and Box enforces it deterministically, whether the agent calls tools directly, through the Model Context Protocol (MCP), or by generating code. Box works with any model and any agent framework, so an agent can operate in your project without reaching files and services you didn’t allow.

Find where your agent breaks before customers do. Red teaming in Strands Evals runs adversarial conversations, such as prompt injections and jailbreak attempts, against your agent and shows the messages and tool calls where it failed. Strands Evals can now also score structured output field by field, giving partial credit when an agent gets most fields right. Use them to fix weak spots before an agent reaches production. To get started, see the Strands Evals documentation.

Cut the cost of routine agent decisions. Strands Decider, the small, open source decision model we featured in last month’s recap, now comes in four sizes built on Gemma 4. Instead of generating text, it picks between options you define, such as which tool to call or where to route a request. When an Amazon team switched ticket classification in one of its largest internal ticketing systems to Decider, estimated cost per ticket dropped by about 98 percent. Average response time dropped by 78 percent.

Get started

Explore Amazon Bedrock, deploy agents with the AgentCore CLI, or build your first agent with the Strands Harness SDK.

Interested in learning how Amazon Bedrock can support your team? Connect with us to start the conversation.

entries.title: The attendee’s guide to the AWS re:Invent 2026 AI/ML track
entries.summary: AWS re:Invent 2026 includes more than 140 AI/ML track sessions. This attendee's guide helps you find the breakouts, chalk talks, workshops, and builders' sessions that fit your role and goals, spanning AI chips, models and inference, agents, agent trust, and sustainability, so you can build a smarter re:Invent schedule.
entries.content:
Artificial Intelligence

The attendee’s guide to the AWS re:Invent 2026 AI/ML track

From November 30th to December 4th, Amazon Web Services (AWS) will hold its annual premier learning event: re:Invent. At this event, attendees will become stronger and more proficient in various areas of AWS technology through a variety of experiences: keynotes given by AWS leaders, interactive working sessions led by AWS experts, and fun, immersive activities such as live entertainment and games at re:Play.

There are over 2,000 learning sessions that focus on specific topics at various skill levels, and the AI/ML (AIM) track has more than 140 unique sessions for you to choose from. We’re here to help you identify the sessions that best fit your needs. Even if you can’t join in person, you can catch up with many of the sessions on demand and even watch the keynotes live.

The basics: Session types

If you can join us, then remember that we offer several types of sessions that can help maximize your learning in a variety of AWS topics.

re:Invent attendees can choose to attend breakouts, chalk talks, builder sessions, workshops, and code talks. The breakout sessions are recorded and uploaded a few days after to the AWS Events YouTube channel, while the rest are live non-recorded interactive sessions. Here are the details for each session type:

  • Breakout sessions: Attendees are in a lecture-style 60-minute informative session presented by AWS experts, customers, and partners.
  • Chalk-talk sessions: Attendees interact with presenters, asking questions, and using a whiteboard in session.
  • Builder sessions: Attendees participate in a one-hour session and build something.
  • Workshop sessions: Attendees join a two-hour interactive session where you work in a small team to solve a real problem using AWS services.
  • Code talk sessions: Attendees participate in engaging code-focused sessions where an expert leads a live coding session.
  • Lightning talk sessions: Attendees watch a 20-minute demo dedicated to either a specific service or customer story (located in the Venetian Expo Hall or Wynn/Encore Upper Convention Promenade).

With so many sessions to pick from, it helps to know how the pieces fit together. Here is how AWS thinks about its AI offerings, so you can decide where to begin and where to focus.

The AWS AI stack overview and tie-in to re:Invent sessions

AWS offers a comprehensive AI portfolio in the cloud. It covers everything from the physical infrastructure and AI chips that power AI workloads up through ready-to-use agentic solutions that teams can adopt today. Understanding how these services work together helps you navigate re:Invent and focus on the sessions most relevant to what you’re building.

Global Infrastructure – It all starts with data centers designed and optimized for AI workloads. These facilities are built to handle the power, cooling, and networking demands that large AI training and inference jobs require.

AI Chips – Running inside those data centers are two compute options: AWS Trainium, purpose-built for high-performance AI training and inference, and NVIDIA GPUs for teams that need GPU-based acceleration. Customers choose based on their workload, performance requirements, and cost targets.

Data Foundation – AI is only as good as the data behind it. AWS Context connects your data across storage, databases, analytics, and search services, giving models and agents access to the right information at the right time.

Models, Training, and Inferencing – This is where models get built, trained, fine-tuned, and served. Amazon Bedrock gives you managed access to hundreds of leading models from multiple providers through a unified API. Amazon SageMaker AI gives you full control to train, fine-tune, and deploy custom models on dedicated infrastructure. Many customers use both depending on the workload.

Agent Development and Management – Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is where you build, deploy, and manage AI agents. It supports any model or provider mix, including models from both Amazon Bedrock and SageMaker AI, so teams can design agents that pick the right model for each task without being locked into a single provider.

Agentic Solutions – At the top of the stack sit purpose-built agents that are ready to use. Kiro helps developers ship correctly the first time with spec-driven development. AWS Quick connects your applications, tools, and data into a personal knowledge graph that learns how you work. Amazon Connect delivers agents for customer experience, hiring, supply chain, and healthcare. AWS Marketplace gives you access to partner-built AI solutions.

Security, Governance, and Cost Optimization run across every layer of the AI stack. They are built into the foundation, with hardware-level isolation at the chip layer and controls that enforce what agents can access and do.

The AI-focused sessions at re:Invent span the full stack. Whether you’re evaluating AI chips, serving models in production, building custom models, deploying agents, or adopting ready-to-use solutions, this guide helps you find the sessions that matter most. Use it to build a smarter re:Invent schedule.

The artificial intelligence and machine learning (AI/ML) track primarily focuses on three core layers of this stack: AI chips, models, training, and inference, and agent development and management, with security, governance, and cost optimization woven throughout. The following sections start at the chip layer and move up through models and agents. Then come sessions that tie the stack together. The guide ends with other relevant topics, such as sustainability and infrastructure where you run your AI workloads. Within each section, sessions for newcomers come first and technical deep dives come last.

Want to skip ahead? Jump straight to the topic you care about:

AWS AI platform sessions

These sessions cover the core AWS AI services together: Amazon Bedrock, Amazon SageMaker AI, Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, and the AI chips that they run on. They help you make architecture choices that still work as your usage grows.

New to AI on AWS? Start with AIM204. It walks through the whole stack. You will see Trainium and Graviton chips, model inference on Amazon Bedrock and SageMaker AI, and production agents on AgentCore. If you’re already building, try AIM364. It helps you choose between Amazon Bedrock and SageMaker AI, and shows when to use both. The example is a real agentic coding app that runs on AgentCore.

Other sessions dig into specific production problems. If you own data strategy, attend AIM363. This chalk talk shows how governed data products feed customization, inference, and agents. It also explains why cost levers like prompt caching, distillation, and batch inference work better on clean data. Need to prove the value of AI? AIM319 looks past cost to business impact. A live demo across the AI stack shows how to measure return on investment (ROI) and compare cost per outcome.

Experienced builders should look at AIM443. In this 400-level chalk talk, you build a training pipeline on Amazon SageMaker HyperPod. You bring in company data and keep governance in place. Then you deploy the same model to Amazon Bedrock for inference or to AgentCore for agents.

AI chips: NVIDIA GPUs and AWS Trainium

AWS gives you two main choices of AI chips for training and inference: NVIDIA GPUs and AWS Trainium. Start with the one you use today, then explore the other.

NVIDIA GPU sessions

AWS offers a wide range of Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) instances with NVIDIA GPUs. These sessions show how to run AI training and inference on them securely and reliably.

Start with AIM2210 for the latest on GPU instances. In AIM3301, a customer shares how it gets the most from its GPU capacity by optimizing GPU scheduling. AIM392 explains when EC2 G7e and G7 instances are a good fit in place of P-series instances. Want to tune AI infrastructure with self-managed agents? Join AIM346.

If you prefer hands-on learning, try AIM345 on disaggregated inference serving. In AIM344, you find the cause of real GPU cluster failures and how to recover from them. In the AIM347 workshop, you can practice GPU performance engineering.

For data processing, see AIM3312. It shows how Amazon EMR with the NVIDIA cuDF plugin for Apache Spark runs jobs up to 3.7x faster on EC2 G7 instances than on comparable CPU instances without code change. The session also covers DuckDB on GPUs.

AWS Trainium sessions

AWS Trainium is a family of AI chips purpose-built for next-generation deep learning training and inference. It delivers high performance at lower cost. Trainium runs on AWS Neuron, the software stack that connects Trainium to familiar frameworks like PyTorch, so teams build without rewrites. Customers who adopt Trainium-based Amazon EC2 instances may see better price performance than comparable instances.

If you’re new to Trainium, AIM211 is the place to start. It traces the full stack, beginning with the silicon and working up to the application. For the latest system, AIM310 shows how Trainium3 and the Trn3 UltraServer keep large mixture-of-experts models performant. If you’re still evaluating transitioning to Trainium3, the AIM2213 panel gathers four AI leaders who have already shipped real products on Trainium.

Several sessions are built around specific roles. Scientists and researchers who live in PyTorch should bring their questions to AIM339, a nanochat code talk, before getting hands-on in the AIM334 distributed-training workshop. ML engineers and developers can architect a production AI assistant with Hugging Face models in AIM349, and get hands-on with inference scaling in the AIM326 workshop. Performance engineers chasing peak throughput will want AIM329 on agentic optimization loops, followed by INV511, a 500-level look inside the Neuron Kernel Interface for serious kernel designers. If you want to run Trainium on Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS), AIM311 whiteboards a resiliency stack that holds up across deployments as large as twenty thousand accelerators. If you deploy through SageMaker AI instead, see the SageMaker AI section.

For those who want to go further, world models are an emerging class that power simulation in gaming, robotics, and autonomous driving. AIM323 is a good starting point and covers serving world models with native PyTorch. From there, pick a hands-on path. In AIM304 you will deploy and optimize a real-time video world model using agentic Neuron workflows, while in AIM305 you will train vision-language-action models for physical AI. Both are builders’ sessions.

Amazon SageMaker AI sessions

Amazon SageMaker AI is the AWS service for customizing and deploying your own models. It handles the whole model lifecycle in one place. You can prepare data and customize a model on serverless compute. When you need more power, you can grow training jobs to thousands of accelerators. After your model is ready, deploy it on SageMaker inference endpoints or SageMaker HyperPod. You keep the model weights, and you decide where your models run.

New to SageMaker AI? Start with AIM342. It shows how to build, customize, and deploy models with one service. Between sessions, stop by the Builder’s Hub and test your skills in one of three contests. Fine tune an agent, field a team in the Agentic Football Cup, or teach a robot a new task. For the latest on robotics, world models, and physical AI, hear a panel of builders in AIM2215. Still picking a model or learning to write evaluations? AIM2205 shows how to build evaluations on your own data. It also shows how to turn business knowledge into models that cost less to run.

Customization starts with data. The AIM434 workshop shows how to prepare datasets for custom models. Next, AIM362 helps you pick the right compute for customization. Then fine-tune and deploy a large language model (LLM) in a few hours in AIM402. Customers will share their lessons too. In AIM393, Salesforce explains how it built and served its Koa models with open weights. Intuit tells its story in AIM361. If you build agents, AIM325 shows how to fine-tune agents that reason, using multi-turn reinforcement learning. The AIM456 workshop links evaluation, fine-tuning, and reinforcement learning into one pipeline. It spans SageMaker AI and Amazon Bedrock.

And if you’re building domain-specific AI, you should join AIM2205. Learn how to test models on your own data and weigh quality against cost. The session also covers when customizing a model is worth it. In AIM398, watch the team behind Forge whiteboard a fast path to building tailored AI solutions, drawing on their end-to-end customer engagements. They will cover everything from setting the right evaluations and optimizing prompts, context, and inference serving to choosing a customization approach that modifies model weights during pre- or post-training. When you’re ready to grow training and inference, SageMaker HyperPod helps you get more from every GPU hour. Teams use it for specialized work like biology foundation models (FMs), physical AI, world models, and sovereign AI. Start with customers who push the limits. In AIM343, Tencent Games explains how it scaled to 1,000 GPUs. In AIM433, HUMAIN shows how it keeps GPU use high for both training and inference.

For hands-on practice, build foundation model pipelines with Amazon EKS in AIM406, or tune AI pipelines with Ray in the AIM403 builders’ session. The AIM435 code talk teaches policy distillation, which trains a small model from a larger one. Physical AI teams can join the AIM318 workshop. It shows how to keep vision-language model training running when nodes fail. Robotics and autonomous vehicle teams can build a physical AI model factory on SageMaker HyperPod in AIM413.

When it’s time to serve your models, two 200-level talks show inference in production. In AIM213, CrowdStrike explains how it runs LLM inference for threat detection with less operational work. In AIM214, Vanguard shares how it trains and serves custom LLMs on SageMaker HyperPod. To build agents on open-weight models with fast inference, try AIM405. To create fast, resilient inference endpoints, join the AIM404 workshop. Platform teams can practice governed ModelOps in the AIM348 builders’ session. They can also add observability with managed MLflow in the AIM408 workshop.

Build and run AI applications and agents with Amazon Bedrock

The model and inference approach you choose shapes what your AI app can do for users. Amazon Bedrock gives you a wide choice of models and helps you pick the right one for each task. It gives you the performance, security, and cost control to run AI apps in production. Some apps need to use tools and data, remember context, and act for you. For those, Amazon Bedrock AgentCore helps you build, connect, and improve agents.

New to Amazon Bedrock? Start with AIM220. It covers what’s new in models, inference, security, and cost management. Then build and deploy your first Amazon Bedrock app in the hands-on AIM317 workshop.

Next, think about the kind of workload you need to serve. A customer support app may need fast answers. A large document processing job may care more about cost and can wait for results. AIM448 helps you pick the Amazon Bedrock inference option that fits your needs. It weighs performance, capacity, cost, and data residency. If your app must reason across your company’s information, attend AIM308. In this session, you’ll build a knowledge assistant that finds answers across documents, images, structured data, and the links between them.

Your inference plan also needs to stay affordable as usage grows. AIM437 helps you decide when to cache repeated context, route requests between models, or move work to batch inference. Model choice matters too. The newest model isn’t always the right one, and switching can change quality, speed, cost, and behavior. AIM438 shows how to test candidate models on your own use cases so you can switch with confidence. After your app is live, AIM374 covers the metrics, alarms, and operating habits to bring into production. Systems specialists can go deeper in INV517. This 500-level session looks at the scheduling and parallelism methods behind efficient large-model inference.

If you want to build an agent, start with the full production picture rather than building infrastructure one piece at a time. AIM212 introduces the complete AgentCore lifecycle. Nasdaq also shares how it runs agents in a regulated industry. For a hands-on path, try AIM439. You start with a basic customer support agent. Then you add memory, tool access, identity, policies, observability, and evaluation until it’s ready for production. Ready to design a multi-agent system? AIM407 uses Strands Agents to coordinate specialized agents. You share state, handle failures, and deploy the result to AgentCore.

After your agent is running, look at what happens under the hood. Each planning step, retrieval, tool call, and retry can add another model call. That changes cost, speed, and reliability. AIM429 connects agent design to inference behavior. It helps you think through context, harnesses, goals, and when an agent should stop. Developers who want to see these tradeoffs in code should follow it with AIM454. That session builds function calling, multi-step reasoning, and retrieval live.

The stakes rise as agents serve more users and reach more systems. Bring your scaling questions to AIM436, where you work through traffic spikes, tool failures, model timeouts, and multi-tenancy. Platform teams that manage agents across a company should attend AIM303. It covers how to find agents, control tool access, manage identity, and see your whole fleet. If your priority is securing every step between a user request and an agent action, pair it with AIM370. Then use AIM440 to turn production traces and evaluations into a steady way to improve agent quality.

Finally, pick a session that looks like the work you want an agent to do. AIM340 follows PepsiCo’s conversational ordering agent. It shows how memory, company APIs, and controls work together in a customer-facing workflow. AIM369 focuses on agents that respond to business events and run processes to the end, with human approval where needed. Software teams can get hands-on in AIM416. There, coding agents move off the laptop and run long-lived, parallel workflows on AgentCore.

Build AI that works with documents, voice, and images

AI apps often need to handle more than text. These sessions show how to build those skills on AWS. They add grounding, evaluation, and verification so your app holds up in real use. For document processing, start with AIM216 on Amazon Textract. Then, in AIM442, build a pipeline that turns documents into structured data you can check. Building voice apps? AIM217 introduces Amazon Polly and Amazon Transcribe, and AIM218 explores conversational AI with Amazon Nova Sonic. Go deeper with the AIM356 code talk, or build and deploy a voice agent in AIM352.

Build cross-modal search in AIM357. To improve quality, add web grounding in AIM350 and automated evaluation in AIM351. You can also explore identity verification with Amazon Rekognition in AIM355.

Building trust in AI agents

AI agents now do real work, like approving claims, issuing refunds, and acting on customer data. Teams need a way to trust what those agents do and prove it to others. That starts with responsible AI, which helps organizations make careful choices about how AI systems are designed, built, and run. AWS builds on that with Trust in Depth. It’s an approach for giving agents more freedom without losing control.

If you’re new to AI trust, start with the AIM2216 panel. It covers how to build confidence at each stage of an agent’s life. Topics include keeping an agent limited to its job and seeing exactly what it did. To see responsible AI governance in practice, attend AIM391. It shows how John Deere used AI Risk Intelligence to replace periodic manual reviews with continuous, automated governance. The change cut assessment time by more than 30 percent.

Several sessions are built for specific roles. Developers can join the AIM336 workshop to audit a multi-agent claims system for responsible AI gaps. Then they fix what they find and write a report backed by evidence. Risk, compliance, and data science teams can join AIM332. This chalk talk covers testing whether agents treat people fairly when they approve loans or issue refunds. You learn how to choose fairness metrics and catch bias in outcomes that affect people’s lives. Do your agents decide things like insurance eligibility? The AIM335 workshop shows how to turn the rules behind those decisions into Automated Reasoning checks in Amazon Bedrock Guardrails. Each decision can then be proven correct and audited.

For a deeper look at the science, several expert sessions cover automated reasoning. INV508 shows how subject matter experts can turn legal and regulatory policies into rules a machine can check. No coding is needed, and those rules then serve as AI guardrails. INV526 looks at what can be proven about agent behavior today, and where the limits are. The AIM451 chalk talk shows how to enforce rules that agents can’t get around. It also shows how to keep people involved in decisions machines shouldn’t make alone.

Other topics

A few more tracks round out your re:Invent planning, from sustainability to where you run your workloads.

AWS Sustainability

AWS is continuously innovating across its data centers, chips, and AI services to be more efficient and sustainable. AWS also gives you the data and tools to measure, track, and reduce the environmental impact of your own cloud and AI workloads running on AWS. These sessions discuss how we’re making our infrastructure more efficient and show how to act on sustainability data while still meeting your business goals. For the latest on the AWS Sustainability service, attend AIM201. This lightning talk covers new impact areas beyond carbon, more detailed data, and API access. In AIM205, learn how AWS makes AI infrastructure more sustainable. It uses hardware with low embodied carbon, energy-efficient custom chips, and data centers tuned by machine learning (ML). Want to understand the method behind your carbon data? Join the AIM321 chalk talk. It shows how to use that data to build AI workloads with a smaller footprint, which often cost less too.

If you prefer hands-on learning, try AIM320. You build a generative AI pipeline with Amazon Bedrock that turns messy company data into sustainability insights. The session is based on how AWS handles life cycle assessment across its data centers. To go deeper, join AIM412. It uses Amazon Neptune and an Amazon Bedrock agent to map how stakeholders depend on each other. You then test ways to cut carbon on a knowledge graph.

Local Zones and AWS AI Factories

As teams move AI into production, where a workload runs matters as much as how it’s built. Large training jobs, fine-tuning, and real-time inference each need different things from infrastructure. AWS gives you several places to run them: AWS Regions, AWS Local Zones, AWS Dedicated Local Zones, AWS AI Factories, and AWS Outposts. Start with HMC303. It compares these options on the four factors that drive the choice: latency, data sovereignty, compute density, and scale. Databricks shares how it uses GPU capacity in select Local Zones. T-Mobile covers latency-sensitive distributed inference.

In HMC307, see how Netflix supports its visual effects and animation teams from the Los Angeles Local Zone. Netflix starts Amazon EC2 G7e instances with NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 GPUs just in time. That way, artists get ComfyUI environments when they need them.

Two hands-on workshops take different paths to building agents at the edge. HMC402 takes the managed route. You connect Amazon Bedrock AgentCore agents in an AWS Region to tools and agents in hybrid and edge locations. You use Model Context Protocol (MCP) and agent-to-agent (A2A) communication. HMC403 takes the self-managed path. You design, set up, and tune your own agents across Local Zones and Outposts. Then learn how to orchestrate fractional GPUs across the edge with NVIDIA Run:ai in the HMC401 code talk.

Some organizations can’t move AI workloads to the public cloud at all. Data sovereignty, data gravity, or latency can stand in the way. AIM206 shows how AWS AI Factories bring AWS and NVIDIA AI infrastructure into your own data center. AWS runs and updates it for you. See how organizations run leading foundation models on premises for training and inference, while keeping full control of their data.

Plan your re:Invent

Use this guide to build your schedule. Then reserve your seats in the event catalog early, since popular sessions fill up fast. Pro tip: if sessions are showing as full in the online session catalog, we recommend favoriting the session and trying your luck by walking up to the session to see if any extra room has become available. There are other activities where you can learn about AWS AI/ML offerings.

Visit the AI kiosks

Between sessions, stop by the AI kiosks at the AWS Village in the Venetian’s Expo Hall. Each kiosk is run by AWS experts who focus on the topics covered, including product managers and solutions architects. They answer your questions, help you think through your use case, and run demos all day. When visiting the AWS Village, come visit these kiosks:

  • Amazon Bedrock.
  • Amazon Bedrock AgentCore.
  • Amazon Foundation Models.
  • Speech AI.
  • Accelerated Computing.
  • Strands Agents.
  • AI League.
  • Amazon SageMaker AI.
  • Global Infrastructure & Sustainability.
  • Hybrid Cloud & Edge Computing.

Try the activations

You can also get hands-on at four interactive experiences, also in the AWS Village in the Venetian’s Expo Hall:

  • AWS Quick: See how work changes when AI agents join everyday operations. Watch solutions architects show Quick live at one of three live demo stations, or go through a demo on your own at one of three self-guided stations. You can also use the touchscreen knowledge graph to explore re:Invent content and sessions.
  • Galactic Agents: Sit down at one of four builder stations to build a five-officer AI crew, then launch your starship. Your crew keeps exploring a shared galaxy on its own all week, even while you’re in sessions. Each officer maps to a real agent pattern that companies use. A giant live galaxy map and a look under the hood show how to run agents you can watch and trust on AWS. Curious how the game was built? Talk to the expert at the SME desk.
  • Security at Machine Speed: Play a touchscreen tabletop game at one of two tables. You protect your cloud and earn points for each AWS security service you deploy. When you finish, visit the nearby security kiosks for deeper conversations.
  • AWS Cloud Infrastructure: Don’t miss the infrastructure experience at the AWS Village. See the hardware behind the AWS Cloud, built on more than 20 years of cloud infrastructure innovation. A chip wall shows every generation of AWS Graviton, AWS Trainium, AWS Inferentia, and AWS Nitro Cards. Touchscreens explain how these chips work with partner chips for agentic AI, training, and inference. Get up close to Trainium and Graviton server trays and racks, and learn how they scale out with Elastic Fabric Adapter (EFA) and Amazon EC2 UltraClusters. Then explore a 3D model of AWS AI Factories to see how AWS brings its infrastructure into your own data center. It’s a good stop after the AI chips, AWS AI Factories, and Local Zones sessions.

Can’t make it to Las Vegas? Watch the keynotes live and catch the breakout sessions later on the AWS Events YouTube channel. We hope to see you at re:Invent 2026.

entries.title: Automating AWS Agent Registry updates with push-based architecture
entries.summary: This post shows how to keep the AWS Agent Registry current automatically. Using AWS CloudTrail, Amazon EventBridge, AWS Lambda, and AgentCore Identity, an event-driven pipeline detects MCP server changes and pushes updated tool metadata to the registry with no stored secrets, across single- and multi-account environments.
entries.content:
Artificial Intelligence

Automating AWS Agent Registry updates with push-based architecture

Every time a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server published in the AWS Agent Registry, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, gains a new tool or updates its schema, the registry record must be updated too. Without automated push-based sync, consumers discover stale metadata. For organizations managing multiple MCP servers across accounts, such a sync keeps catalog records current within an existing governance workflow.

In most enterprise deployments, a catalog’s value depends on its freshness. If a developer deploys a new tool on Monday, but the registry record still reflects last week’s schema, consumers lose trust in the catalog. Stale metadata directly reduces registry reliability, leading teams to inadvertently build dependencies on inaccurate information.

When an engineer adds a tool to an MCP server but forgets to update the catalog:

  • Consumers miss out on the new capability entirely.
  • Applications might call the tool using an outdated schema, causing unexpected runtime behavior or silent workflow deviations.

Multiplied across teams, this lack of automation erodes trust in the registry. Organizations ultimately fall back on ad hoc discovery mechanisms like hardcoded endpoints, informal knowledge sharing, and stale documentation.

In this post, we outline an event-driven architecture that automates these updates using AWS CloudTrail, Amazon EventBridge, and AWS Lambda.

Architecture overview

The following solution brings these services together into an event-driven pipeline that detects runtime changes and synchronizes them to the registry automatically.

The architecture supports both multi-account and single-account environments:

  • Single-account setup: For straightforward deployments, all components reside within Account A. Cross-account forwarding setup isn’t needed as events flow directly within Account A.
  • Multi-account setup: This involves two accounts where runtime events from Account B are securely forwarded to Account A.
    • Account A (registry account) owns the AWS Agent Registry, the Amazon EventBridge rule, the push-sync Lambda function, and CloudTrail logs.
    • Account B (MCP server account) hosts the MCP server runtime and the Amazon Cognito OAuth provider used for authentication.

The sample uses two accounts, but you can scale the architecture for multiple accounts, with Account A as the registry account and multiple AWS accounts similar to Account B for different MCP servers.

The following diagram shows the end-to-end event flow for an update to an MCP server in Account B. The captured event is forwarded to Account A, where a Lambda function queries the MCP server for its tools and updates the matching registry record.

The architecture uses five AWS services:

  • AWS CloudTrail captures 
    UpdateAgentRuntime
    API calls as management events.
  • Amazon EventBridge routes matching events to the Lambda function, with cross-account forwarding supported.
  • AWS Lambda queries the MCP server for its current tools, diffs against the registry, and updates the record if changed.
  • AWS Agent Registry stores MCP server records and their tool schemas as the central source of truth.
  • AgentCore Identity, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, brokers OAuth token exchanges securely, so the Lambda authenticates without storing secrets.

How it works: business logic flow

After it’s deployed, the pipeline runs the following end-to-end workflow:

  • Trigger: A developer in Account B updates an MCP server, which calls the 
    UpdateAgentRuntime
    API in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, and AWS CloudTrail captures the event.
  • Route: Amazon EventBridge catches the CloudTrail event and forwards it to the central event bus in Account A.
  • Parse: The sync Lambda in Account A extracts the runtime Amazon Resource Name (ARN) from the event payload and dynamically constructs the MCP server’s invocation URL. This is how it knows which server in Account B to query.
  • Authenticate: The Lambda generates a secure OAuth bearer token through AgentCore Identity.
  • Fetch: The Lambda calls the MCP server (
    initialize
    , then 
    tools/list
    ) to retrieve the latest tools information.
  • Sync: The Lambda finds the matching registry record by its ARN, evaluates the differences, and updates the registry if the schema has changed.

This flow assumes that the Agent Registry in Account A already contains a pre-registered record for the MCP server (created during initial onboarding). The Lambda function in this sample updates existing records only. It doesn’t generate new ones.

This same flow works in a single-account setup where all resources (registry, Lambda, Amazon EventBridge rule, and MCP server) reside in one account. In that case, skip the cross-account forwarding step. Events flow directly within the same account’s Amazon EventBridge bus.

Technical walkthrough

This section walks through the workflow for a single MCP server update with two accounts as depicted in the architecture diagram.

The same flow executes independently for each server that emits an 

UpdateAgentRuntime
event. The Lambda handles one event at a time, scaling naturally with the Amazon EventBridge invocation model.

Step 1: Event capture and routing for cross-account setup

When a developer deploys or updates an MCP server, the 

UpdateAgentRuntime
API is called, either by the AgentCore CLI (
agentcore deploy
) or directly.

AWS CloudTrail records this as a management event in Account B, with a delivery delay of approximately 5–15 minutes. The event is then delivered to Account A’s default Amazon EventBridge bus.

For a cross-account setup, Account B’s Amazon EventBridge forwards matching events to Account A’s event bus through a cross-account rule.

The Amazon EventBridge rule target in Account A invokes the sync Lambda, passing the full CloudTrail event JSON as the input payload.

The Amazon EventBridge rule pattern:

Step 2: Extract the MCP server URL

The Lambda parses the runtime ARN from the event. It extracts the hosting Account ID and AWS Region to dynamically construct the target MCP server’s URL-encoded invocation endpoint.

Step 3: Secure authentication with AgentCore Identity

The Lambda authenticates using a two-step identity flow. It exchanges its execution identity for a temporary workload token. The Lambda then trades this token for a scoped OAuth bearer token through the target account’s credential provider.

Credential providers are per-account (

CREDENTIAL_PROVIDER_{ACCT_ID}
), so one Lambda authenticates MCP servers across multiple accounts.

Step 4: Query the MCP server

Using standard MCP streamable-HTTP mechanics, the Lambda establishes an active session through an 

initialize
request. After the session is active, it calls 
tools/list
to fetch the complete array of currently exposed tools and schemas.

Step 5: Find the matching registry record

The Lambda queries the central Agent Registry to locate the corresponding record. It searches APPROVED records for one whose 

mcpServer.data
contains the runtime ARN embedded during record creation (see the Deployment section).

Step 6: Diff and update

To minimize unnecessary writes, tool lists are normalized (sorted by name, compared using name + description + inputSchema). The registry update only fires when a change is detected. If the schemas differ, the Lambda logs the exact additions or removals and pushes the fresh definitions to the registry record.

Governance and approval workflow

AWS Agent Registry enforces a governance lifecycle on each record: Draft -> Pending Approval -> Approved (or Rejected/Deprecated). Administrators configure approval settings at the registry level. These settings control what gets published, who reviews it, and whether records require manual approval before becoming discoverable. Only records in Approved status are visible to consumers through search, catalog browsing, or the registry’s MCP endpoint.

When the Lambda updates a record with new tool definitions, the record automatically reverts to Draft status. Consumers continue to see the previously approved version. A curator or administrator must then approve the update before the new metadata becomes discoverable. This way the automated updates cannot bypass organizational review, and administrators retain full control over what is exposed to consumers.

Deployment

The following table outlines steps in the automation pipeline:

StepDescription
Define configurationRegion, Lambda name, registry ID, and MCP server ARN
Create and approve registry recordRegister the MCP server entry and move it to APPROVED
Provision AgentCore IdentityCreate workload identity and OAuth2 credential providers
Deploy Lambda functionCreate IAM execution role, package handler, deploy function
Create Amazon EventBridge ruleRoute 
UpdateAgentRuntime
events to the Lambda
Cross-account forwarding (optional)Forward runtime events from remote accounts

Prerequisites

Before deploying this solution, verify that the following are in place:

  • An AWS account with permissions to create Lambda functions, Amazon EventBridge rules, AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) roles, and Agent Registry resources.
  • AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) configured with credentials to access all the services used in the sample. For more information, see Getting started with the AWS CLI.
  • Python 3.12 runtime.
  • An existing AWS Agent Registry with at least one MCP server record (created during initial onboarding; instructions to create the record are provided in the Deployment section).
  • An MCP server deployed on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime.
  • An AgentCore Identity workload identity and OAuth2 credential providers configured for each MCP server account (see sample repository for setup).
  • For multi-account setups, cross-account Amazon EventBridge permissions between Account B and Account A.

Organizations often use multiple accounts, where the registry is in one account but the MCP servers are in others. This sample outlines the multi-account scenario, which you can convert to a single-account scenario by following the instructions.

Creating the registry record

In this sample, before the sync pipeline can work, a registry record must exist with the runtime ARN explicitly embedded in its server schema. You can use the following code to create the registry record and include the runtime ARN in the record’s 

mcpServer.data
field. This is what the Lambda matches against to correlate AWS CloudTrail events to records:

Approving the record

The Lambda only syncs to APPROVED records.

After making the update, the registry record is in the DRAFT stage. It must move through the governance workflow for the change to be discoverable.

Lambda environment variables

To maintain a strong security posture, zero client secrets are stored in the Lambda environment variables. The function relies entirely on mapping environment variables to reference runtime workload identities, provider names, and permission scopes.

Amazon EventBridge rule

This rule acts as the pipeline trigger, listening for 

UpdateAgentRuntime
management events within the local account or arriving from cross-account Amazon EventBridge bus forwarders:

Clean up

To avoid ongoing charges, delete the following resources when you are done:

  • Lambda function – Delete the push-sync Lambda and its IAM execution role.
  • Amazon EventBridge rule – Delete the rule and its Lambda target.
  • AgentCore Identity – Delete the workload identity and OAuth2 credential providers.
  • Registry record – Delete or deprecate the test MCP server record.
  • Registry – Delete the registry if it was created solely for testing.
  • (Multi-account) Remove the cross-account Amazon EventBridge rule and resource policy in Account B.

You can find the cleanup code in the sample repository.

Known limitations and future improvements

The sample code outlined here (and in the full sample) can be extended in several ways:

  • Automatic registration of new MCP servers – Currently, a matching registry record must already exist. A future enhancement could automatically create a record when a previously unknown MCP server is detected for the first time.
  • Manual “force sync” trigger – For time-sensitive deployments, an on-demand invocation path through Amazon API Gateway or a CLI command can serve changes outside the regular CloudTrail delivery flow.
  • Cold-start resilience – If an MCP server is cold and returns zero tools, the Lambda currently doesn’t retry. Adding exponential backoff and skipping the update when the tool count is zero would improve reliability.

Conclusion

The AWS Agent Registry gives organizations a governed, discoverable catalog for their AI agents and MCP servers.

The push-sync Lambda pattern closes the freshness gap: when a server change is detected, the registry record is updated automatically and securely, within the constraints described in the Known limitations section. Updates revert the record to DRAFT status and must pass through the approval workflow before becoming discoverable again.

As your agent fleet grows from a handful to hundreds of MCP servers, this pattern keeps your registry as the single source of truth, consistently fresh and reviewed.

Get started

The full implementation (Lambda code, deployment script, and architecture diagram) is available as a ready-to-deploy sample. To deploy the solution in your environment, clone the repository and follow the deployment steps in the README.

entries.title: How DXC Technology built a multi-model AI substrate on Amazon Bedrock
entries.summary: DXC Technology runs mission-critical managed IT services for regulated organizations across 70 countries. Learn how DXC built DCX OASIS, its Human+AI operating model, on a governed multi-model substrate in Amazon Bedrock, separating a resilient model substrate from a trusted harness that orchestrates, governs, and audits AI agents at scale.
entries.content:
Artificial Intelligence

How DXC Technology built a multi-model AI substrate on Amazon Bedrock

This post is co-written with Nick Tamburro of DXC Technology.

When an AI agent can act on a production server at a bank or a hospital, access to a capable foundation model is only the starting point. Recent public incidents, in which autonomous agents took destructive actions their operators never intended, show that the real risk is rarely the model alone. It’s an agent holding more authority than its task requires, with nothing in the architecture to stop it. Avoiding that starts with a substrate that governs model access at the infrastructure level.

Amazon Bedrock provides that substrate. Through a single managed interface, it gives DXC OASIS access to multiple foundation models: Anthropic Claude, Amazon Nova, Meta Llama, and open-weight families. Amazon Bedrock Guardrails enforce content filtering, personally identifiable information (PII) redaction, and denied-topic policies uniformly across every model. AWS PrivateLink keeps inference traffic within the customer’s virtual private cloud (VPC), and serverless scaling avoids self-managed GPU infrastructure as a failure point. Because these are system-level controls rather than bolt-ons, they gave DXC Technology a governed foundation for what no model layer can deliver on its own: a trusted harness that orchestrates, governs, and audits AI agents across enterprise IT operations at scale.

Model availability varies by AWS Region. See Supported models by AWS Region in Amazon Bedrock.

DXC Technology runs managed IT services for some of the world’s most regulated organizations: banks, hospitals, and government agencies. With more than 115,000 employees across 70 countries, DXC operates mission-critical systems where resilience and governance are non-negotiable. When DXC set out to build DXC OASIS, the harness for mission-critical IT operations, the team separated the problem into two layers. The first is a governed model substrate built on Amazon Bedrock. The second is the trusted harness built on top: DXC’s own orchestration, governance, and assurance layer.

In this post, we explore how DXC built the resilient, flexible model substrate beneath DXC OASIS on Amazon Bedrock. We also show where DXC drew the line between what the substrate provides and what the harness must provide. Since general availability in March 2026, DXC OASIS has reduced resolution time by 95% on average across 56 measured use cases.

Across every model, customer data stays within the AWS data boundary: prompts and completions are not shared with third-party model providers and are not used to train the underlying foundation models.

“Our customers operate complex, business-critical environments and need both choice and resilience in how they adopt AI. Amazon Bedrock provides access to a broad ecosystem of models with the governance, security, and operational controls required at enterprise scale. That flexibility allows us to use the right model for the right task, adapt as technology evolves, and stay focused on delivering measurable business outcomes for our customers.”

— Dan Gray, President, GIS, DXC Technology

Solution overview

DXC OASIS separates the question of which model from the question of how work gets done. Amazon Bedrock is the substrate: a governed gateway to foundation models (FMs), reachable through one consistent API, with security and networking controls that keep traffic inside the AWS perimeter. The harness is everything DXC builds on top: orchestration across tools and systems, operational context drawn from 60 years of runbooks and escalation logic, policy enforcement, human-oversight gates, and full auditability of every agent action.

The design goals were:

  • Resilience: No single point of failure at the model layer.
  • Flexibility: Route each task to the most appropriate model on cost, latency, and capability.
  • Regulatory sovereignty: Meet the data-handling expectations of regulated tenants.
  • Safety by design: Bound what every agent can do, so that no action with operational impact runs without policy checks and, where required, human approval.

The main risk DXC designed against was coupling the system to any single provider, framework, or deployment target. The following diagram shows the key AWS services in the DXC DXC OASIS architecture.

Engineers and operators reach the system through Amazon Route 53 and an Application Load Balancer inside the customer’s Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (Amazon VPC). The DXC OASIS agent runtime runs on Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) in a private subnet. There, a supervisor agent delegates to capability agents that draw on a knowledge base, AWS Secrets Manager, Amazon EventBridge, and Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3). Every model call leaves the subnet through a VPC interface endpoint and AWS PrivateLink to reach Amazon Bedrock, so inference traffic doesn’t traverse the public internet. AWS Identity and Access Management (AWS IAM), AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS), TLS 1.2, Amazon CloudWatch, VPC Flow Logs, AWS CloudTrail, and OpenTelemetry provide security and observability across every layer.

Building the DXC OASIS substrate

DXC began building DXC OASIS as a prototype in early 2025. A cross-functional team reached general availability in March 2026, scaling toward 130 customer environments on Amazon EKS with per-tenant namespaces and GitOps rollout. Building the substrate involved the following tasks:

  • Establish governed, multi-model access through Amazon Bedrock.
  • Engineer resilience into every layer of the architecture.
  • Route each workload to the most appropriate model.
  • Draw the line between the substrate and the harness.

Establish governed, multi-model access through Amazon Bedrock

Every model DXC OASIS uses (Anthropic Claude, Amazon Nova, Meta Llama, and open-weight families) is reached through Amazon Bedrock model inference. A provider outage or deprecation therefore becomes a routing decision, not a system rebuild. Uniform access isn’t the same as uniform behavior, however: models differ in capability, response style, and failure modes. Substituting one model for another is an assurance activity as much as a routing change. Before a model enters production routing, the harness (not the API) evaluates it against DXC OASIS task suites. For more information, see Getting started with Amazon Bedrock.

Engineer resilience into every layer

Resilience in DXC OASIS isn’t one control but the compounding of several. The following table summarizes the resilience controls and what each does for DXC OASIS.

Resilience controlWhat it does for DXC OASIS
No single-provider dependencyEvery model is reached through Amazon Bedrock model inference. A provider outage or deprecation is a routing decision rather than a system rebuild, with the harness assuring behavioral differences between models before a switch goes live.
Serverless model layerAmazon Bedrock is serverless and the Amazon EKS control plane is AWS managed, removing single points of failure.
Scope-of-impact containmentAmazon Bedrock Guardrails apply content filters, denied topics, PII filters, and contextual controls consistently regardless of model, containing the scope of any single failure.
Private, encrypted pathsAmazon VPC and AWS PrivateLink keep model traffic off the public internet. TLS 1.2 in transit and AWS KMS at rest protect data.
Elastic capacityAmazon EKS autoscaling with per-tenant namespaces makes onboarding a new tenant a capacity-planning exercise.

Beyond resilience, DXC OASIS also addresses data residency and sovereignty. Regional inference controls and AWS PrivateLink keep inference within approved AWS Regions and off the public internet, meeting the data-handling expectations of regulated tenants.

Route each workload to the most appropriate model

The strategic reason DXC built on Amazon Bedrock is optionality. Because every model sits behind the same API, the team routes each task to the most appropriate model on cost, latency, and capability, and adopts new frontier models as they arrive without re-plumbing the system.

Model choice as a workload decision

Each task’s capability, latency, and cost requirements determine which model it uses, not system constraints.

Intelligent prompt routing – A single serverless endpoint predicts response quality and routes requests between models in the same family. It sends simpler prompts to lower-cost models and complex reasoning to more capable ones. Prompt caching further cuts latency and cost. For more information, see Intelligent prompt routing in the Amazon Bedrock documentation.

Custom model import – With Custom Model Import, the same governance and tooling extend to models that DXC or its clients bring themselves.

Open and closed models together

Amazon Bedrock supports open-weight models alongside proprietary ones, so DXC pairs frontier reasoning with open-weight models a client can adapt and deploy under one set of guardrails.

Draw the line between the substrate and the harness

Every enterprise agent needs six capabilities. Some are substrate capabilities Amazon Bedrock provides directly. Others are things only the harness can provide because they depend on DXC’s operational context and accountability model. This boundary is also where agent safety is won or lost. Guardrails on model inputs and outputs are necessary, but only the harness can limit what an agent is allowed to do. The following table draws that line.

CapabilityWhat Bedrock providesWhat the harness adds
OrchestrationA foundational service layer the harness calls, wraps, or extends.Supervisor and capability-agent delegation across tools, systems, and multi-step workflows, built on the open source LangGraph runtime.
ContextKnowledge-base infrastructure and prompt caching for retrieval.60 years of runbooks, escalation logic, and live IT service management (ITSM) data.
GovernanceAWS IAM, regional inference controls, and tenant-isolated model access.Per-request policy enforcement, persona-based authorization, and field-level constraints.
GuardrailsAmazon Bedrock Guardrails: content filters, denied topics, PII filters.Operational-policy enforcement above the substrate filters: tiered knowledge hierarchy, scoped and auditable agent roles, and customer-specific rules on what an agent can act on.
Human oversightNot a substrate function.Four authority tiers (observe, propose, act with approval, act within scope), with every persona starting read-only, plus approval gates and escalation paths.
AssuranceEncryption, auditable infrastructure, and VPC Flow Logs.OpenTelemetry traces for every action, each with a unique execution ID, giving end-to-end traceability from intent to action.

How a workload flows through DXC OASIS

To make the architecture concrete, the following use cases come from the DXC OASIS demo environment. The environment is built around AnyCompany Airlines, a fictional mid-sized airline running a hybrid on-premises and AWS estate.

  • Incident resolution: Diagnose and fix an at-risk production server, from alert to resolution in under 10 minutes.
  • Problem management: The ITSM agent ranks the top five incident categories and suggests how to reduce each, work that takes 2–3 hours by hand.
  • Cloud cost analysis: For the AWS cloud engineer, the Metrics agent breaks down a 90-day cost trend by service and region, then investigates spending peaks on request.

The incident-resolution workflow shows how the substrate and the harness work together:
