  • Alert in business terms – A runbook fails to clear disk space on the FlightOps server. The CIO sees the alert as a business risk: Flight Operations scheduling might be affected within 4 hours. At the same moment, the Linux engineer sees the same alert with the technical detail needed to act.
  • Plan and delegate – The engineer opens AI Assist from the dashboard widget, and the metric carries into the chat as context. A supervisor agent breaks the request into a plan and delegates to capability agents (DXC OASIS Metrics, Linux System, and ITSM), with every model call made through Amazon Bedrock.
  • Grounded diagnosis – The DXC OASIS Metrics agent confirms the server is 99% full and cites the knowledge base articles behind its answer. The Linux System agent traces the problem to a single 5 GB temporary file.
  • Human approval – The agent presents its full execution plan, and nothing runs until the engineer confirms it. In this workflow, the agent operates at the act-with-approval tier: it can diagnose freely, but it can’t change the production server without an explicit, recorded approval.
  • Governed execution – The fix runs, and DXC OASIS records what ran, on which server, who approved it, and when. The audit trail comes from the harness, not from the agent’s own account of what it did.
  • Learn and observe – The engineer can turn the conversation into a draft knowledge article. The Query Metrics view shows the agent timeline, delegation flow, and token usage behind the answer.

Results

Since reaching general availability in March 2026, DXC OASIS agents now serve 12 operational personas, spanning Linux, Windows, SAP, virtualization, backup and patching, AWS, Azure, and network operations. Across 56 measured use cases, DXC OASIS has reduced resolution time by 95 percent on average. The following table shows representative measurements.

TaskBeforeAfterTime saved
Filesystem incident53–90 mins3–6 mins~89–97%
Database performance incident2–3 hours5–12 mins~90–97%
Cloud policy validation4–8 hours15–30 mins~88–97%
Patching validation45–90 mins5–10 mins~85–90%
Complex problem management2–6 days8–10 mins~99%

Diagnostic accuracy is 92% or better, validated against senior engineer judgment.

Lessons learned and what comes next

Four architectural decisions proved most valuable:

Separate model choice from orchestration

By keeping model selection, orchestration framework, and deployment target as independent decisions, DXC avoids re-platforming when a layer evolves.

Compound resilience controls

No single control makes the system resilient. The combination of serverless infrastructure, guardrails at the model layer, private networking, and human-oversight gates creates defense in depth.

Draw the substrate-harness line explicitly

Clarity about what the cloud provides versus what you must build avoids both under-engineering (trusting the model to govern itself) and over-engineering (rebuilding capabilities the substrate already offers).

Bound autonomy before you scale it. Every DXC OASIS persona starts read-only, and broader authority is granted deliberately, one tier at a time. Treating autonomy as something granted per task, rather than a default, is what lets DXC put agents in front of production systems with confidence.

Bound autonomy before you scale it

Every DXC OASIS persona starts read-only and broader authority is granted deliberately, one tier at a time. Treating autonomy as something granted per task, rather than a default, is what lets DXC put agents in front of production systems with confidence.

Looking ahead, DXC is evaluating Amazon Bedrock AgentCore alongside the current orchestration layer, and expanding the system to support additional regulated workloads as new frontier models become available through Amazon Bedrock.

Conclusion

In this post, we showed how DXC Technology built DXC OASIS, the harness for mission-critical IT operations, on a governed, multi-model substrate in Amazon Bedrock. Keeping model reasoning separate from operational orchestration builds resilience, flexibility, and regulatory compliance into the architecture from the start. The payoff is measurable: resolution time is down 95 percent on average across 56 measured use cases. For teams building their own agentic systems, the lesson is to treat the substrate (what Amazon Bedrock provides) and the harness (what you build on top) as separate layers. Decide early which capabilities belong in each. As scrutiny of autonomous AI grows, that clear line, together with bounded, auditable agent authority, is what lets a system earn trust at scale.

To get started with multi-model architectures on Amazon Bedrock, see the Amazon Bedrock User Guide. To learn more about how DXC OASIS applies this architecture to enterprise IT operations, contact DXC Technology.

entries.content:
Artificial Intelligence

Accelerating generative AI delivery with reusable assets

If you’re building generative AI solutions, reusable assets can help you stop rebuilding components that already exist: Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) pipelines, document processors, agent scaffolding, and so on. This has a compounding cost: time not spent solving the customer’s actual problem.

This post shows you how to access a curated catalog of 23 production-ready assets from the AWS Generative AI Innovation Center, now part of AWS Frontier AI Engineering & Services. These assets can reduce your development time from months to weeks, with evidence from companies like DoorDash, Lyft, and Ricoh.

Since 2023, the AWS Generative AI Innovation Center has published open source reusable assets. These production-grade building blocks give you a validated foundation to start from instead of a blank file. These assets have powered customer solutions delivering measurable results: 50x increases in testing capacity, 90 percent reductions in engineering hours, and deployment timelines compressed from months to weeks. In this post, you will learn why teams keep rebuilding generative AI components, what makes an asset truly reusable, how companies like DoorDash and Ricoh achieved measurable results by using these assets, and how to access and deploy 23 open source assets from the catalog. For a complete list of all available assets, see the asset catalog at the end of this post.

The problem: Why teams keep rebuilding

Three root causes drive redundant development across generative AI teams:

  • No single source of truth – Assets scatter across repositories, wikis, and drives. Builders can’t find what exists, so they rebuild from scratch.
  • No quality signal – Without verification of production readiness, security reviews, or maintenance status, builders have no way to trust existing solutions and default to writing their own code.
  • No reuse culture – Sharing remains informal and ungoverned. What one team builds stays with that team, and problems get solved repeatedly.

The cost of rebuilding compounds. Each redundant build consumes engineering hours, delays customer delivery, and creates maintenance burden. Even AI-generated code requires production hardening, security reviews, testing at scale, and ongoing maintenance. These assets arrive already validated, security-reviewed, and production-grade, avoiding that verification burden. When teams finally reach production, they’ve spent weeks on undifferentiated heavy lifting, work that should have been reusable from day one. The AWS Frontier AI Engineering & Services resolves this challenge through reusable assets.

What a reusable asset actually is

A reusable asset isn’t a code snippet or a sample. It’s a production-grade, composable building block that implements a discrete generative AI capability. Reusable assets are validated for quality and security before publication. They include clear deployment guides for discoverability and are instrumented to track adoption across customer engagements. These assets are maintained across their lifecycle.

Examples from the catalog include RAG pipeline components, document ingestion modules, agent scaffolding templates, evaluation frameworks, and prompt management patterns. The assets are tested in production environments, reviewed for security compliance, and refined based on real customer feedback.

This is the difference between a one-off artifact and a building block you can trust.

Real results: Customer success stories

The value of reusable assets isn’t theoretical. Here’s what happens when teams build on proven foundations instead of starting from scratch.

Contact Center GenAI Agent: DoorDash and Lyft

According to the AWS case study, DoorDash built a fully voice-operated self-service generative AI contact center solution using the Contact Center GenAI Agent asset. As reported, the solution handles over 100,000 calls per day with 2.5-second response latency, achieving a 50x increase in testing capacity. Using Amazon Bedrock reduced development time by 50 percent. The team reached live testing readiness in 2 months.

Lyft used the same Contact Center GenAI Agent asset to bring agentic AI to life for riders and drivers, demonstrating the asset’s versatility across different customer engagement models.

The Contact Center GenAI Agent provides automated question answering capabilities for both text and voice channels. It employs a RAG architecture to facilitate multi-turn conversations while maintaining context. The solution integrates with Amazon Connect and uses Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases, a fully managed RAG capability, for hybrid search and metadata filtering.

Learn more:

GenAI Intelligent Document Processing: Ricoh

Ricoh serves major health insurance payers, managed care organizations, and healthcare providers. These customers process hundreds of thousands of critical documents each month, including insurance claims, grievances, appeals, and clinical records. As Ricoh scaled to serve more healthcare customers, they needed a standardized, multi-tenant document processing approach. That approach had to onboard new implementations without requiring unique development and tuning for each one.

Using the Accelerated Intelligent Document Processing on AWS asset as a foundation, Ricoh built a standardized, multi-tenant solution for automated document classification and extraction. This transformed their document processing from a custom-engineering bottleneck into a scalable, repeatable service.

Results: As documented in the published case study, Ricoh achieved a 7-fold throughput increase, from 10,000–70,000 documents monthly. Engineering hours per deployment dropped by over 90 percent (80 hours to under 5). Onboarding time fell from 4–6 weeks to 2–3 days. The system now processes 1,000 documents in minutes during traffic spikes, delivering over 1,900 potential annual person-hours in savings.

The GenAI IDP Accelerator, introduced in this 2025 blog post, is a scalable, serverless solution for automated document processing and information extraction using AWS services. This system combines optical character recognition (OCR) with generative AI to convert unstructured documents into structured data at scale. The AWS Frontier AI Engineering & Services continuously maintains the assets as well.

Learn more:

  • Blog post: AWS GenAI Intelligent Document Processing (IDP) Accelerator
  • Blog post: How Ricoh built a scalable intelligent document processing solution on AWS.

New assets: Building the future of agentic AI

Reusable assets become more valuable as teams shift focus from infrastructure to business logic. Two recently launched assets demonstrate how reusable building blocks can accelerate the development of next-generation agentic applications.

Fullstack AgentCore Solution Template (FAST)

The Fullstack AgentCore Solution Template (FAST) is a starter project repository. With FAST, you can quickly deploy a secured React frontend connected to Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale with any framework or model. In this implementation, FAST uses a React-based frontend with the managed infrastructure of AgentCore to accelerate building full-stack agentic applications from weeks to days.

FAST deploys in under 30 minutes using infrastructure as code (IaC), with built-in integrations for AgentCore memory, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, along with Gateway, Code Interpreter, and Observability. Authentication uses Amazon Cognito, configured with enterprise security best practices, and the template is designed for AI-assisted development with extensive documentation and steering docs.

With FAST, you can access a complete reference architecture that shows you how the pieces integrate, with a working full stack application that you can learn from and build upon. With the modular design, you can swap out major components (identity providers, frontend frameworks, hosting solutions, or agent frameworks) as your requirements evolve.

Learn more:

  • FullStack AgentCore Solution Template
  • Accelerate agentic application development with a full-stack starter template for Amazon Bedrock AgentCore

Agentic Chatbot Accelerator

The Agentic Chatbot Accelerator is a web application deployment solution that uses the AWS Cloud Development Kit (AWS CDK) for infrastructure as code so you can create agentic chatbots. Built on Strands Agents and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, this solution streamlines the development of agentic chatbot applications.

The accelerator provides rapid deployment using AWS CDK, with scalable agent runtime management through Strands Agents and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. It is configurable and extensible for diverse chatbot use cases, with pre-configured patterns for authentication, hosting, and scaling, validated across customer deployments.

Learn more:

Walkthrough: Using an asset from the library

Let’s walk through a concrete example of selecting and using the Contact Center GenAI Agent asset from the open source catalog.

Prerequisites

To follow this walkthrough, you need:

  • An AWS account with permissions to create AWS CloudFormation stacks, Amazon Connect instances, Amazon Bedrock resources, and Amazon Quick Sight dashboards.
  • AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) installed and configured with appropriate credentials.
  • An Amazon Connect instance (or permissions to create one).
  • Access to Anthropic Claude Sonnet and Anthropic Claude Haiku on Amazon Bedrock.
  • A Jupyter notebook environment for validation testing.

The scenario

You’re building a customer support solution that needs to handle both voice and text interactions, answer questions using your company’s knowledge base, and escalate complex issues to human agents.

Finding the asset

Navigate to Contact Center GenAI Agent on GitHub. The README provides a clear overview of capabilities, architecture, and deployment steps. The following figure shows the solution architecture for the Contact Center GenAI Agent.

Evaluating the asset

The asset includes security-reviewed code with AWS CDK infrastructure as code, integration with Amazon Connect for voice and chat, and Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases, a fully managed RAG capability, for question answering. An automated testing framework and conversation analytics dashboard are built in.

Responsible-AI controls are integral to the architecture. Amazon Bedrock Guardrails enforces production-grade safety controls, including hallucination detection, content filtering, and topic-level boundaries, making sure agents operate within defined safety parameters from day one.

The repository shows active maintenance, comprehensive documentation, and links to customer success stories (DoorDash, Lyft) that validate production readiness.

Deploying the solution

Deployment follows four steps:

  • Clone the repository and install dependencies.
  • Deploy two AWS CloudFormation templates: one for the Knowledge Base stack and one for the RAG solution stack.
  • Integrate with Amazon Connect using the pre-built contact flows included in the repository.
  • Validate the deployment using the included Jupyter notebooks.

The full process takes under an hour. The solution also includes an Amazon Quick Sight dashboard for real-time conversation analytics.

For detailed deployment instructions and prerequisites, see the deployment guide.

Clean up

To avoid ongoing charges, delete the resources created during this walkthrough. The deployment uses two AWS CloudFormation stacks, so deletion follows the reverse order:

  • Delete the RAG solution stack from the AWS CloudFormation console.
  • Delete the Knowledge Base stack from the AWS CloudFormation console.
  • Remove the Amazon Connect contact flows created during integration.
  • Delete the Amazon Quick Sight dashboard and any associated SPICE datasets.
  • For detailed cleanup instructions, see the deployment guide.

The outcome

Instead of spending weeks building a contact center solution from scratch, you can deploy a security-reviewed, tested foundation in days. Your team focuses on customizing the knowledge base, refining prompts for your domain, and integrating with your existing systems. This is the high-value work that differentiates your solution.

Potential time saved: 4–6 weeks of development time

What you focus on instead: Domain-specific customization, prompt engineering, business logic integration

Access to the AWS Generative AI Innovation Center open source assets

You can access 23 reusable assets as open source on GitHub and AWS Labs. Each asset includes deployment guides, sample code, and documentation to help you get started quickly.

Document processing and extraction

  • Multi-lingual Document Processor (MDP) – Transforms complex multi-modal documents into structured text.
  • Intelligent Document Processing with Generative AI – Extract information from custom documents.
  • Extracting Information From Complex Documents – Hands-on workshop for document extraction.

Contact center and voice

  • Live Call Analytics with Agent Assist (LCA) – Real-time generative AI for customer and agent voice calls.
  • Contact Center: Post Call Analytics (PCA) – Generative AI analysis of post-call recordings.
  • Live Meeting Assistant (LMA) – Captures audio from browser-based meetings with transcription and insights.
  • Recorded Voice Insight Extraction Webapp (ReVIEW) – Upload recordings and use generative AI to answer questions.

Agentic AI and chatbots

  • Agentic Chatbot Accelerator – Web application deployment for agentic chatbots.
  • Fashion Assistant Agent – Fashion assistant built with Amazon Titan on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore.
  • Natural Language Database Agent – Query databases using natural language with LangGraph.

RAG and knowledge bases

  • Leveraging the User to Improve Agents in RAG Use Cases – Custom LangChain tool for conversational RAG.
  • Reranker Fine-Tuning and Deployment – Fine-tune BAAI BGE Reranker for improved retrieval.
  • Durable Semantic Caching in Amazon MemoryDB – Persistent semantic caching for GenAI applications.

Development and migration

  • C to Java Code Conversion – Agentic workflow for legacy code migration.
  • OpenAI Migration Framework – Systematic framework for large language model (LLM) migration.
  • Fine-tuning ModernBERT for Intent Classification – Create smart LLM routing systems.

Infrastructure and operations

To get started:

  • Select one of the assets listed earlier.
  • Review the README and deployment guides for assets relevant to your use case.
  • Clone the repository and follow the deployment instructions.
  • Customize the asset for your specific requirements.
  • Reach out to the AWS Frontier AI Engineering & Services team for advisory support.

Conclusion

The cost of rebuilding is real, and it compounds. When teams rebuild RAG pipelines, recreate document processing logic, or start from scratch, those hours add up in engineering time that could have been spent solving actual customer problems.

A curated, validated asset catalog changes the economics of generative AI delivery. Not by doing the work for you, but by making sure you’re not doing work that’s already been done. The 23 open source assets published since 2023 represent thousands of engineering hours, dozens of customer engagements, and countless lessons learned. They’re packaged into building blocks you can deploy today.

The assets are open source. The deployment guides are comprehensive. The customer’s success stories are real. Start with one asset that matches your current challenge. For expert assistance, reach out to the AWS Generative AI Innovation Center.

entries.summary: Learn how to build an AI-driven product development lifecycle (AI-PDLC) with a suite of six AWS Quick agents that take you from scattered customer signals to a validated prototype across Discover, Decide, Design, and Prototype, with human approval at every gate and a specification ready to hand to coding agents like Kiro.
entries.content:
Artificial Intelligence

Accelerating product development with AI-driven lifecycle management (AI-PDLC) in AWS Quick

This blog post focuses on how AI can improve and expedite the product development life cycle using agents built on AWS Quick, with human approval baked into the process.

AI-driven software delivery is helping teams ship products faster than ever. As implementation accelerates, the upstream product development process becomes even more important. Coding agents can turn clear requirements into working software faster than before, but they can’t compensate for building the wrong product. With implementation becoming easier, your competitive advantage moves upstream to four critical activities: discovering the right customer problem, deciding which opportunity to pursue, designing the right experience, and validating it through a prototype.

The signals that you need to make those decisions are scattered everywhere. Your customers leave feedback in Slack, your sales team logs insights in Salesforce, systems record incidents in ServiceNow, stakeholders document requirements in Microsoft SharePoint, engineers track work items in Jira, and teams make decisions in Outlook meetings and email threads. As your teams move between these tools, they disconnect context from the decisions it should inform, and lose more at every handoff.

AWS Quick provides the connective layer for this fragmented knowledge. By grounding custom chat agents in connected enterprise data and storing their artifacts in shared Spaces, AWS Quick helps your team build with existing organizational knowledge instead of starting each initiative from a blank page.

The AI-Driven Product Development Lifecycle (AI-PDLC) is a framework that applies these capabilities through a suite of six AWS Quick agents with specialized skills, producing a traceable set of artifacts at each phase. Agents gather and structure context, surface gaps, and draft artifacts. You and your team contribute judgment and approve every decision. The objective isn’t to produce documents faster. It’s to help your team think better, preserve why each decision was made, and give engineering and coding agents a specification grounded in customer evidence. We will show you how to configure the six-agent AI-PDLC suite in AWS Quick and use it to move from distributed customer signals to a validated prototype. Throughout, it preserves context from the first insight through the engineering handoff.

Architecture

The diagram shows the end-to-end flow of the AI-PDLC framework.

It starts with the signals most teams lose track of, that is, the Slack threads, Jira tickets, docs, and call transcripts that hold the why behind a decision and what customers actually said. Enterprise connectors pull that context from Slack, Outlook, Jira, Salesforce, SharePoint, ServiceNow, and many more enterprise sources.

AWS Quick can build a personal knowledge graph from your connected apps and folders, linking the people, projects, and decisions across your tools.

Those signals feed the brain: the set of agents on AWS Quick, led by an Orchestrator that runs Discovery, Prioritize, Working Backwards, Spec Generator, and Designer. Everything they produce lands in one common language: a 

prototype_spec.md
holding the acceptance criteria, personas, screens, data model. Every decision traces back to a source.

AWS Quick can delegate development tasks to AI coding agents using the Agent Client Protocol (ACP). ACP is an open JSON-RPC 2.0 standard with no vendor lock-in. Customers can use their preferred coding agent like Kiro or Claude Code to build against the specification generated by AI-PDLC.

Underneath it all runs a human approval gate at every stage. You validate the pain points, approve priorities, sign off the spec, gate the build, and accept the review. Production data then flows back into Discovery, closing the loop. The agents do the work while you make the calls, and nobody has to leave their tool to do it.

Solution overview

The AI-PDLC lifecycle spans eight phases: Discover, Decide, Design, Prototype, Engineer, Ship, Operate, and Learn. This post focuses on the first four, where the product team works. The last four are handled by coding agents such as Kiro, which build from the specifications the upstream phases produce. The upstream phases are implemented as six agents in AWS Quick.

Users interact only with an Orchestrator, which reads each specialist’s question framework at runtime, asks targeted questions for the current phase, and dispatches artifact generation to the right specialist. A single conversation drives the whole journey, and the pipeline advances only after human approval at each step in the workflow.

Phase 1: Discover

The Discovery agent guides structured pain point analysis across interactive Q&A, URL ingestion, and direct pulls from connected enterprise sources like Slack, Jira, support tickets, Salesforce, and research repositories. It scores every pain point for severity and frequency, producing a Pain Point Board that gives the team one evidence-grounded view of what customers struggle with.

Phase 2: Decide

The Prioritize agent scores each use case against weighted criteria using two transparent 0–10 frameworks: one purpose-built for agentic use cases (large language model (LLM) capability match, tool availability, user acceptance) and one for traditional applications (feasibility, business impact, effort). The team can open the Scoring Matrix and trace exactly why one use case outranks another.

Once the top use case is selected, the Working Backwards agent generates a full PR/FAQ using the Amazon Working Backwards method with customer FAQs and internal FAQs covering unit economics, failure modes, regulatory risk, and competitive landscape. If a concept can’t survive this scrutiny, the team learns that on paper before committing engineering resources.

Phase 3: Design

The Spec Generator agent turns the validated use case and PR/FAQ into a build-ready specification, with separate templates for agentic versus application use cases plus a Design Handoff Brief for UX teams. Each spec contains acceptance criteria, user flow, constraints, and metadata that traces every requirement back to its source pain point, prioritization score, and the PR/FAQ that validated it. Those acceptance criteria serve a dual purpose: they’re the build contract the coding agent follows, and the review rubric the review agent audits against. What used to take multiple sprints of drafting and review becomes a focused session, detailed enough for engineering to build from design spec immediately, with few or no clarifying meetings required.

Phase 4: Prototype

The Designer agent generates journey maps, wireframes, and clickable HTML prototypes directly inside AWS Quick. It works from the Design Handoff Brief, personas from Discovery, user flow from the PR/FAQ, screens to design, brand context, and the emotional target drawn from the customer quote, so teams can validate concepts with stakeholders before committing to Figma or other design tooling. After the spec is approved, it’s dispatched to the engineering team for development.

The entire loop is iterative, with humans reviewing and approving at every gate. Nothing ships without explicit signoff. What traditionally takes multiple weeks of prototyping and iteration could become days or even just hours of guided agent collaboration depending on the complexity of the problems.

Every decision is logged at two levels. Each specialist records its own decisions, scores, and rationale inside the artifact it produces, and the Orchestrator independently checks that those entries exist while keeping a shared log across the whole pipeline. If one layer slips, the other still holds a complete record, so no gate approval goes untracked.

AI-PDLC can be executed across two pacing modes. Deep Discovery asks 8–12 questions per phase, chasing ambiguities and edge cases. It fits a new problem space where the team wants thorough exploration. Fast Track trims each phase to 3–5 essential questions and suggests defaults from context it already holds, letting you confirm or override each one. It fits time-boxed sessions where the team knows the space and needs to move quickly.

Agent implementation details: Step by step

We will walk through the details of the agent creation and implementation process.

Prerequisites

  • An AWS Quick workspace with the Desktop client installed.
  • Access to create custom agents in AWS Quick with Enterprise connectors configured for Slack, Jira, SharePoint, or other tools your team uses.

Step 1: Clone the AI-PDLC repository

The full agent suite, reference architecture, prompt templates, and setup instructions are available in the AI-PDLC GitHub repository.

The repository contains:

  • Agent instruction files for all six agents.
  • Question framework samples for each specialist agent.
  • Configuration files and setup guide.

Step 2: Create the specialist agents

In AWS Quick, create the specialist agents using the instructions from the repository:

Step 2.1: Download the JSON file from the GitHub repository for agent building.

Step 2.2: Go to Quick Desktop → Customize → Agents → Create, then choose Create from File.

Step 2.3: The chat window opens up.

Step 2.4: The following six agents with instructions are created:

The Orchestrator is the central architectural component. It dynamically reads each specialist’s instructions at runtime:

Step 3: Configure Quick Spaces (artifact repository)

Create a shared Quick Space for storing pipeline artifacts:

  • Open Quick Spaces and select Create New Space.
  • Name: AI-PDLC Artifacts.
  • Grant access to relevant team members.

Step 4: Run the pipeline

  • Open AWS Quick Desktop.
  • Select AI-PDLC Orchestrator from the agent picker.
  • Enter: “Run the full pipeline” (or “Fast Track” for an abbreviated session).
  • Answer the Orchestrator’s structured questions as it guides you through each phase.
  • Review artifacts as they are produced at each gate.

You can select the pace, Deep Discovery or Fast Track, based on your needs.

Watch it in action

For a live demonstration of AI-PDLC in action, from customer insight through all four phases to a working prototype, watch our YouTube video walkthrough:

  • YouTube Part 1: End-to-end product lifecycle with AWS Quick and AI coding agents (51:49)
  • YouTube Part 2: Creating AI-PDLC agents

The video covers:

  • Setting up the agent suite.
  • Running the full Orchestrator pipeline through a real-world use case.
  • Real-time artifact generation in action.
  • The ACP handoff to coding agents.
  • Tips for choosing between Deep Discovery and Fast Track modes.

AI-PDLC scenarios

We will walk through some common scenarios where the AI-PDLC framework can be applied:

Scenario 1: New product development, starting from scratch

When a team identifies a new market opportunity or unmet customer needs, they face the classic cold-start problem: scattered signals, competing ideas, and no structured way to move from insight to action. AI-PDLC guides the team through the full upstream journey, surfacing pain points from real customer data and scoring competing ideas against transparent criteria. It also validates the concept through a rigorous PR/FAQ and produces a build-ready spec so the first line of code is written against a validated plan, not a hunch.

Scenario 2: Feature addition to an existing product, roadmap-driven or customer-driven

Product teams continuously receive signals that inform what to build next: customer feedback in support channels, feature requests from sales, usage data showing dropoff points, or strategic priorities from leadership. AI-PDLC accelerates this by pulling those signals from connected tools (Slack, Jira, Salesforce, AWS Quick Sight). The framework structures them into a prioritized backlog with evidence-backed scoring and produces a spec that preserves the “why” behind each feature, so engineering receives context-rich work items instead of one-line Jira tickets stripped of intent.

Scenario 3: Bug fixes and incident-driven improvements

When a production issue surfaces through customer complaints, monitoring alerts, or support escalations, the response often skips structured analysis and jumps straight to a code fix. AI-PDLC brings discipline to this reactive workflow by capturing the root cause as a documented pain point, assessing whether the fix warrants a broader design change or a targeted patch. It produces a scoped spec with testable acceptance criteria so the fix addresses the underlying problem rather than just the symptom, and the decision trail is preserved for future reference.

Each scenario follows the same pipeline (Discover → Decide → Design → Prototype) but enters at different depths. New products run the full journey, feature additions may skip deep discovery, and bug fixes may compress to a single focused cycle. The methodology adapts while the audit trail and governance remain consistent regardless.

Clean up

The resources this walkthrough creates incur no cost at rest, so you can safely keep the entire AI-PDLC suite in place if you plan to run the pipeline again.

To remove what you no longer need, delete the six agents under Customize → Agents in Quick Desktop, delete the AI-PDLC Artifacts Space (or just the test artifacts within it) and revoke any team access you granted, and disconnect any Enterprise connectors or coding agent links you added solely for this exercise. You can also remove the cloned GitHub repository from your local machine.

Conclusion

The bottleneck in product development has shifted. Coding agents have made implementation fast. However, the upstream work still constrains teams: discovering customer problems, deciding what to build, validating the concept, and producing clear specifications. Teams that compress this upstream cycle can gain a compounding advantage: they build the right product, faster, with fewer costly pivots.

AI-PDLC addresses this directly. It provides a structured, AI-native framework, implemented as a suite of agents in AWS Quick that guides product teams through Discover, Decide, Design, and Prototype with built-in governance at every gate. AI-PDLC attributes every decision. Every artifact traces back to customer evidence. And when the spec reaches engineering, it carries the full context of why it exists, who validated it, and what “done” looks like.

The product team’s role isn’t to write code. It’s to make the right decisions about what to build and why, quickly and traceably. AI-PDLC makes that possible.

Get started today

  • Clone the repository.
  • Follow the setup guide in the repository to create five specialist agents and one Orchestrator.
  • Select “AI-PDLC Orchestrator” from the agent picker and say: “Run the full pipeline”.
